Title: Presentation to the Annual Conference of the NZ Association of Economists (NZAE)
Subtitle: Bob Buckle, Emeritus Professor, Victoria University of Wellington and an external member of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will give a keynote address at the NZAE conference.
text: i Monetary policy and the benefits and limits of central bank independence Robert A. Buckle Emeritus Professor, Victoria University of Wellington. External Member, Reserve Bank of New Zealand Monetary Policy Committee. Disclaimer: The views expressed in this paper are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of colleagues, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, and other members of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Monetary Policy Committee. Abstract: Central bank independence is an important development in macroeconomics. It has become a lynchpin of modem central banking. The period since the Global Financial Crisis and the experience of the Covid-19 pandemic era posed new challenges for central banks, with potential implications for central bank independence. This paper reviews the scope and rationale for central bank independence and the reasons it spread internationally after the 1980s. It reviews evidence of the effects of central bank independence on inflation, output volatility, financial stability and fiscal policy. The paper considers political threats and contemporary policy issues that could influence the form of central bank independence and credibility. These issues include matters relating to assessments of monetary policy during the pandemic, the scope of central bank mandates, interpretations of inflation dynamics, the funding of central bank operations, and the interaction between fiscal and monetary policy. Presented to the Annual Conference of the New Zealand Association of Economists. 30 June 2023. Introduction It is a great pleasure to be invited to speak at the Annual Conference of the New Zealand Association of Economists (NZAE). I attended my first NZAE conference during the mid- 1970s. At that time, average annual inflation for OECD countries was persistently around 10 per cent, and rising. Four years later it was over 15 per cent and hovered around 8 per cent until the early 1990s. Thereafter, inflation declined and never exceeded 8 per cent for over 30 years, and persisted for long periods between 1 and 3 per cent, until the resurgence after the Covid- 19 pandemic. The containment of inflation for over 30 years in many countries was not a chance event. A transformation in central banking took place during the 1990s. Many countries gave greater operational independence to central banks for monetary policy, supported by novel accountability and transparency requirements. This occurred initially among developed economies, although many developing economies also soon adopted this institutional framework for monetary policy. During this process, inflation declined globally. While other factors contributed to low inflation, central bank independence (CBI) came to be regarded as the crucial foundation for credible monetary policy and persistent low inflation. Central bank independence is an important development in macroeconomics, and is a lynchpin of modern central banking. Nevertheless, confidence in CBI has recently come under strain and in some instances been threatened. Some claim central banks have become far less independent than two decades ago.1 Others are concerned with the expanded role of central banks and implications for their clarity of purpose, adequate accountability and legitimacy.2 Some have suggested central banks have become less focussed on inflation.3 Others have expressed concern over rising political threats to central bank independence, or that the constituency for low inflation has been eroded.4 In extending this invitation, the NZAE Council suggested I speak on the broad developments of a topic in economics or economic policy. In the spirit of that request, I will discuss the background to the emergence of CBI, review its scope and meaning, its spread internationally, and why it was adopted by so many countries. I also will review evidence of the benefits arising from CBI. Finally, I will address some issues that have emerged in recent times relevant to the concerns mentioned above and which have potential implications for central bank independence and monetary policy. 1 See for example, Rogoff (2022), Lingle (2021) 2 See for example, Tucker (2018a), Rajan, (2023). 3 See The Economist (2022). 4 See Goodhart & Lastra (2018a) on rising political threats. The scope and growth of central bank independence Central bank independence refers to the freedom of monetary policymakers from direct political or governmental influence in the conduct of policy.5 This does not involve complete independence from government because legislation specifying the objectives of a central bank are determined by governments. Furthermore, funding, board appointments, and accountability requirements of central banks are determined by governments. There are different elements to CBI and the manner in which they are specified varies across central banks. These elements cover how the central bank aligns with the political process and other organs of government, the financing of a central bank, and the nature of the employment conditions of central bank governors and monetary policy committee members. They cover how the specification of central bank objectives are determined and how policy decisions are formed and approved. They also cover issues relating to the choice of policy instruments (degree of instrument autonomy), and accountability requirements.6 To provide structure to this complexity, attempts have been made to measure the degree of independence using the laws of a country that establish and govern them.7 The most comprehensive attempt are the coding and weighting rules developed by Cukierman, Webb and Neyapti (1992) (CWN), shown in Table 1. The CWN scheme became a widely accepted basis for de jure measures of CBI (although others have been developed and used for research). Reasons why central bank independence spread internationally What prompted this dramatic change in the institutional framework for monetary policy during the 1990s? After all, it seems the performances of early independent central banks were mixed, and the concept had sceptics among influential monetary economists. According to Goodfriend (2012), independent monetary policy originated in the 19th century with the Bank of England and the US Federal Reserve. He considers the Bank of Englands lender of last resort policy served its purpose well, but the Federal Reserve ran monetary policy according to an ill-defined public interest and became a source of macroeconomic instability. In contrast, the independent Bundesbank and Swiss National Bank were relatively successful at achieving persistently low inflation during the post-WW2 decades. This was influential, especially in European Monetary System countries.9 An early contribution to the CBI debate was by Milton Friedman (1962) in his discussion of monetary structures both stable and free from irresponsible government tinkering. He considered three alternatives: a commodity standard, an independent central bank, and legislated rules for monetary aggregates. Friedman was sceptical that an independent central bank could deliver low inflation consistently. He argued it was rare for an independent central bank to not take account of government preferences, and the degree of independence was dependent on the personality of central bank governors. He preferred instead that government legislate rules for the instruments of policy, and specifically for money supply growth. A dramatic change in Federal Reserve policy took place under the leadership of Paul Volcker. In October 1979 the focus shifted toward controlling the money supply with the aim of reducing inflation.10 Annual inflation had risen from 3 to 9 per cent in 18 months and was projected to 8 Cukierman et al. By the end of 1983, the annual inflation rate had been brought down to 4 per cent, and low inflation was sustained until 2021. The Volcker episode showed that monetary policy could achieve a significant reduction in inflation. However, the output and employment costs of this policy were accentuated by weak policy credibility.11 The system was still vulnerable to Friedmans concern of dependence on the personality of central bank governors. The problem was similar to the consequences of the time-inconsistency of optimal plans highlighted by the seminal work of Kydland and Prescott (1977). To overcome this problem and the inflationary bias it created in the context of monetary policy, subsequent literature emphasised the importance of expectations, the credibility of monetary policy, and the benefits of enforced commitments (or rules) over discretion.12 To achieve a credible commitment to low inflation, Rogoff (1985) proposed delegating monetary policy to an independent central bank in order to insulate central bankers from political pressures that could otherwise induce elected politicians to renege on promises of low inflation. It is widely considered that it was not until New Zealand introduced in 1989 a formal arrangement combining operational independence and inflation targeting supported by a high degree of transparency and accountability, that the idea of CBI (and inflation targeting) took flight. This innovation was introduced in New Zealand as part of a wider set of public sector reforms and a search for a solution to persistent high inflation.13 A feature of the legislation was a contractual relationship between the central bank Governor and the Government that changed the incentives of the central bank in a manner consistent with Rogoff s proposal.14 Many features of New Zealands approach influenced central bank governance in other countries. By the late 1990s, a consensus was emerging that the primary aim of monetary policy should be to control inflation and CBI was an effective way to do this.15 Other factors influenced the spread of central bank independence. Research revealing the adverse effects of persistent high inflation motivated the search for a solution to breaking high inflation.16 Public-sector debt ratios in many countries had become much lower in this period which meant that when central banks raised interest rates to reduce inflation, it would have been of less concern for governments.17 The potential for CBI to signal creditworthiness to foreign investors in an environment of more internationally integrated financial markets may have also been a motivation.18 The influence of particular interest groups such as the financial sector which was expanding during the 1990s, may therefore have been important. What have been the benefits of central bank independence? The growth of independent central banks after 1990 was associated with a shift in focus of monetary policy toward inflation targeting.20 Initial interest therefore focussed on the marginal effects of CBI on inflation and, to a lesser extent, output volatility. The effectiveness of monetary policy also depends on the efficiency and stability of financial systems and the cooperation of fiscal authorities. Accordingly, CBI spurred interest in evaluating whether politicians circumvent the discipline of monetary policy independence via financial system regulations and fiscal policy. The research into the marginal effect of central bank independence has evolved considerably and benefitted from the availability of larger samples of countries, improved data on central bank independence, improved econometric estimation techniques and understanding of the importance of other factors that can influence the impact of central bank independence. The following is a flavour of the insights from this research. 4.1. Central bank independence and inflation Evaluation of the marginal impact of CBI on inflation goes back to Bade and Parkin (1978), followed by several other studies in the 1990s.21 The broad conclusion was that CBI resulted in lower inflation, with variation by country coverage and choice of indices of independence. These studies focussed on developed economies and samples were relatively small. Subsequent research extended country coverage, tested components of de jure independence and de facto measures of independence, searched for possible coefficient estimation bias due to not adequately controlling for other influences on inflation, allowing for country specific effects, and improved econometric methods including dynamic panel estimation methods.22 This large volume of research was evaluated by Klomp and de Haan (2010a) using meta-analysis. Although they found results varied by time period, the size of inflation rates, and country coverage, their overall conclusion is that CBI reduces inflation. Significant effects of CBI reducing inflation were found in studies for Latin American countries, democratic developing countries, former communist countries, and in countries with initial high rates of inflation. They revisit this question using a sample of 118 non-OECD countries covering 1980 to 2013, using the CWN approach to measure the degree of CBI.24 They find that in most developing countries, a higher degree of CBI results in lower inflation. The effect is stronger in the presence of more democratic institutions, in the presence of a floating exchange rate, and when a central bank operates under an explicit inflation targeting mandate. The effect of CBI on price stability nevertheless persists after controlling for these effects. The spread of CBI facilitated greater use of monetary policy instruments to supplant the prevalent use of less effective nonmonetary devices to stem the persistent high inflation that characterised the decades prior to the 1990s.25 This is likely to be have been an important factor enabling CBI to achieve sustained lower inflation. 4.2 Central bank independence and output volatility The decades following the initial surge of CBI were characterised by falling volatility of inflation and output growth, coined the Great Moderation by Bernanke (2004). Figure 2 plots at quarterly intervals, the combinations of standard deviations of average annual inflation rates and real output growth for OECD countries. It reveals that volatility of both inflation and output growth were generally higher during the late 1970s and the 1980s. During the subsequent two decades, when central bank independence was spreading globally, inflation and output volatility were on a declining trend. There are cycles about this trend. In the early 2000s, output growth volatility increased (possibly due to spill-over effects of the Asian Financial Crisis and the Dotcom share market crash). This alters the trade-off between inflation and output volatility, and therefore macroeconomic volatility.27 4.3 Central bank independence and financial stability The intersection between monetary and financial conditions means CBI could impact financial stability, though there is debate as to whether CBI fosters or weakens financial stability. Arnone, et al. (2009) and Bernanke (2010) have suggested CBI fosters financial stability. On the other hand, Atkin and Kern (2020) suggest increased CBI resulted in weakening of financial regulation in some countries, as governments sought to compensate for the loss of control of monetary policy and find other ways to expand credit for politically strategic areas. 26 A review of research on contributions to declining output volatility during the Great Moderation is in Buckle, et al. (2003). 27 This point is articulated by Bernanke (2004) who couched his argument within the context of Taylors (1979) monetary policy efficiency frontier. The way improved central bank credibility can change inflation dynamics and improve the Taylor efficiency frontier is explained in Clarida, et al. (1999), Orphanides & Williams (2005a), and Buckle (2019) who also reviews evidence of the impact of CBI and inflation targeting on New Zealands inflation and output volatility. 10 There are various ways CBI and inflation targeting could influence financial stability. A central bank that credibly committed to low inflation may generate more predictable interest rates and lower long-term interest rates and therefore interest rates and asset prices will be more stable.28 There are counter-arguments. An independent central bank that has established a credible low inflation policy may reduce the probability investors and financial institutions assign to economic downturns, which might encourage higher risk investment behaviour.29 The combination of CBI and inflation targeting raised concerns this could result in more abrupt interest rate changes that pose higher financial risks for financial institutions.30 Recent USA bank failures is illustrative of what can happen when policy interest rates are increased rapidly. The empirical research on the effect of CBI on financial stability is more recent, but there is an emerging theme which is that central independence can improve financial stability. Several studies indicate CBI is associated with improved banking stability.31 Others evaluate the impact of CBI on financial stability more broadly using time-series panel models that control for other potential influences. For instance, Klomp and de Haan (2009) cover 75 developed and developing countries from 1985 to 2005 and find that CBI reduces financial instability. Moreover, countries in which central banks have an explicit mandate for financial supervision have improved financial stability. Fouejieu (2017) evaluates developing countries using a composite macro-financial condition index covering the period 2001 to 2010. The results suggest inflation targeting central banks are relatively more sensitive to financial risks. These studies covered years prior to the Global Financial Crisis (GFC). The GFC challenged the view that inflation targeting central banks will give sufficient consideration to financial stability. There are a few studies that take account of the GFC period. These also suggest that CBI contributes to lower financial instability. They show that the effect of CBI in moderating financial instability is more important in countries with high levels of democracy.32 4.4 Central bank independence andfiscal policy Granting independence to a central bank involves politicians foregoing economic policy flexibility. The question that naturally arose when CBI was spreading was whether it would induce more fiscal discipline by governments, or whether the objectives of monetary policy would be compromised by fiscal dominance. If CBI was considered by politicians as part of a broader package of reforms to achieve sustained low inflation and fiscal discipline is deemed part of that broader package, greater fiscal disciple might be an outcome. If on the other hand politicians consider low inflation the sole preserve of the independent central bank thereby easing a constraint on fiscal policy, there may be less fiscal discipline. These motives could result in fiscal dominance reducing the effectiveness of CBI.33 Fiscal dominance can occur when there is conflict over stabilisation policy that results in a competitive game that frustrates the central banks ability to pursue its monetary policy goals.34 It can also occur is when governments generate unsustainable fiscal deficits and public debt that influence expectations of the likelihood of future monetisation of public debt and higher inflation. Perceptions that fiscal policy and public debt levels are not sustainable can therefore compromise current and future monetary policy.35 An early investigation into the relationship between CBI and government budget deficits by Parkin (1987) suggested countries with independent central banks had smaller deficits, although this was not conclusive. Subsequent studies using different indices of central bank independence and different samples of developed and developing countries spanning the years from 1950 to 1992 (years prior to the surge of CBI and low inflation) produce a mix of significant and insignificant effects of CBI on fiscal deficits.36 However, these studies may not adequately capture the full effects of CBI which became more widespread after the early 1990s. There are several studies that cover the years since the expansion of CBI. In general, these studies are more robust in controlling for other influences on fiscal outcomes and suggest budget deficits tend to be smaller when central banks are more independent, but there are important qualifications that have emerged from this research.37 These studies suggest the impact of CBI on fiscal policy is conditioned by domestic political and legal institutions. The influence of CBI on fiscal policy is more effective in democracies and in countries with robust legal systems, a free press, and constraints on the political executive, and less effective in autocratic regimes. The effect appears stronger for those countries that are part of a currency union and share a common central bank, than for countries that have a national central bank. A higher level of financial development also improves fiscal performance and reduces reliance on central bank financing. These studies find evidence of a political cycle effect within democracies. Some contemporary issues for central bank independence In spite of these benefits, there are issues that could threaten or impact the characteristics of central bank independence. These include political threats to CBI, the scope of central bank mandates, funding arrangements, dissatisfaction with central bank responses to the Covid-19 pandemic, and the relationship between monetary and fiscal policies. 5.1 Threats from overt political pressures The status of independent central banks has come under threat from political movements that are discontent with the status quo. Goodhart and Lastra (2018a, p50) suggest this threat is particularly acute when democratically elected politicians try to remove the checks and balances generally applied in a democracy. During the 2017 and 2022 French Presidential campaigns, the candidate for the National Rally Party (Marine Le Pen) was advocating changes to the policy decision making processes and institutions that were interpreted as a threat to the independence of the Banque de France.38 Criticism over timing of response to the post- pandemic inflation prompted an unusually explicit threat by Pierre Poilievre, leader of the Conservative Party of Canada and of the Parliamentary Official Opposition, to remove the Governor of the Central Bank of Canada if elected.39 During the 2016 USA Presidential campaign the Republican candidate (Donald Trump) publicly criticised the then Federal Reserve Chair. As President, he launched a series of public criticisms of the decisions of the Federal Reserve as he embarked on an expansionary fiscal programme.40 The independence of central banks in these countries has to date survived these threats, but this is not the case in Turkey. The coalition Government formed after the 2002 elections and led by Prime Minister Erdogan (and later President) started to lose support after the GFC. As the economic situation deteriorated and democratic processes were eroded, and as the costs of losing power increased, pressure came on the Central Bank of Turkey by the President and his Government to lower interest rates.41 Having repeatedly stated his belief that high interest rates cause inflation, the President dismissed two central bank governors. Under the new Governor Kavcioglu, successive interest rate cuts were implemented. Annual inflation soared to 85.5 per cent by October 2022, and the value of the Turkish lira plummeted.42 The events in Turkey illustrate how central bank monetary policy decisions can be vulnerable to political pressure. While the GFC temporarily increased macroeconomic volatility in many countries, inflation was contained. However, macroeconomic volatility increased even more abruptly during the pandemic era. This is illustrated by Figure 3 which extends Figure 2. Output volatility surged in 2020, and a surge of inflation volatility soon followed. Macroeconomic volatility reached levels not previously experienced in the era of central bank independence. The Covid-19 pandemic posed unprecedented challenges for governments and central banks. Debt is the sum of the following liability categories (as applicable): currency and deposits; debt securities, loans; insurance, pensions and standardised guarantee schemes, and other accounts payable. 26 Moreover, despite some debt reduction in 2022, the prospect is for debt ratios to rise further in the near term. The OECD (2023) expects debt levels of developed economies to increase slightly in 2023 as many countries aim to protect households and businesses from rising prices and as debt servicing costs increase. The current geopolitical environment is adding further uncertainty over future government funding needs. The OECD reports that developing economies also have historically high levels of debt and a challenging funding environment. The combination of high inflation, high nominal interest rates and high public debt levels was a lethal combination for monetary policy to contend with during the 1970s and 1980s. Similar circumstances could arise if central banks struggle to contain the post-pandemic inflation or central bank independence comes under political pressure. There are important reasons to consider improvements to the assignment of fiscal and monetary policies in response to destabilising events. However, higher public debt levels increase the risk of fiscal dominance and higher inflation highlighted by Sargent and Wallace (1984) and reiterated by Leeper (2023). This risk can come through pressures on central banks to reduce interest rates and public debt servicing costs or via pressure to monetise debt. 6. Conclusion Central bank independence spread globally after the 1980s and has become a critical foundation for credible monetary policy and sustained low inflation. Other benefits accruing from CBI, include improved financial stability and lower fiscal deficits outside election years. There are qualifications to these conclusions. The effects of CBI can vary by type of political environment, the economic characteristics of countries, and the presence of other economic policy frameworks such as fiscal frameworks and currency regimes. Despite these benefits, challenges to central bank independence have emerged. The main characteristics and legislated limits to central bank independence include objectives (mandates) and conditions pertaining to objectives, and accountability and transparency requirements. The most critical aspect of central bank independence is discretion over the choice and operation of monetary policy instruments in pursuit of the legislated objectives. This paper suggests there are intersections between legislated objectives and operational independence that could have implications for central bank independence and the political acceptability of CBI. These intersections involve expanding central bank mandates, conditions attached to the pursuit of primary objectives of monetary policy, and funding arrangements that could influence central bank independence over the choice and scope of alternative monetary policy instruments. Although there have been overt political threats to central bank independence, perhaps the more important challenge is how central banks respond to the criticisms that emerged from the extraordinarily difficult circumstances created by the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and the surge of inflation that followed. There are important lessons from this experience including the choice and application of policy instruments, the scope for improving fiscal and monetary policy coordination while protecting central bank operational independence, and insights into the dynamics of inflation. How central banks respond to this 27 experience and the insights will influence the acceptability of central bank independence and the determination of monetary policy. Title: Testing our resilience
Subtitle: A speech delivered by Governor Adrian Orr at INFINZ Conference 2022
text: Testing our resilience. Speech delivered at INFINZ Conference 2022 Adrian Orr, Governor 27 October 2022 Reserve Bank of New Zealand xx Te Putea Matua Tena koutou katoa. Thank you for the opportunity to talk today and it is pleasing that it is in person following a series of virtual meetings in recent times. It is also a privilege to be presenting here alongside the Financial Markets Authority CEO Samantha Barrass. Our institutions are working increasingly hand-in-hand, which makes complete sense for our financial industry. I am deliberately keeping my remarks high level. You will be hearing from Te Putea Matua multiple times over the coming weeks. Between now and end-November you will be treated to our Financial Stability Report, our 5-yearly Review of our monetary policy activities, our Monetary Policy Statement, and round two of public consultation on the 5-yearly review of our Monetary Policy Remit. The Financial Stability Report to be released next week provides a rich assessment of the financial system and broader economy. The most obvious theme will be the resilience of our financial system to manage through challenging economic times. New Zealand is not unique in facing growing economic challenges - they are global in their making. However, New Zealand is well positioned to manage. Over recent months I have been able to re-engage with many global economic policy makers face-to-face - most recently at the IMF and World Bank joint annual meetings in Washington DC. While people were genuinely pleased to meet in person again, that's where the fun stopped. The content of the meetings was far from positive. Global economic challenges are large and upon us The world economy is experiencing high inflation. This means central banks globally - the Reserve Bank of New Zealand included - are working to actively slow domestic spending by raising interest rates so as to constrain inflation. This means employment prospects will be increasingly compromised, as people delay their spending and investment decisions. The trade-off of the long-run benefits of low and stable inflation versus near-term spending and employment is being confronted in virtually every country simultaneously. Figure 1 provides a timely snapshot of the current inflation and unemployment position across countries. New Zealand is relatively well positioned but inflation is still too high in an absolute sense. Nations who are most impacted by food and energy price spikes and shortages stand out significantly with double-digit inflation rates. The latest available data- points have been used; unemployment data for 2022Q2 for all countries, and inflation data for 2022Q3 for all countries except Costa Rica (CRI) for which only 2021Q4 data is obtainable. Turkey has been omitted since it is an outlier with an exceptionally high inflation rate of 81%. The global coincidence of the monetary policy tightening is not surprising. COVID has been a global shock to the productive capacity of the entire planet. People are worse off for it, and spending plans have been radically disrupted. We are still working through the lingering economic impacts of the lingering virus. How are financial and economic stresses manifesting at present? There was a significant list of concerns repeated in many languages and accents at the recent IMF meetings. The list of near-term pressures goes something like: Returning to low inflation will, in the near-term, constrain employment growth and lead to a rise in unemployment. The actual extent of this trade-off remains unclear however, given the significant labour shortages globally and the very different means of employment being adopted post- COVID. Importantly, it is highly unlikely that we are at maximum sustainable employment if inflation is still high and variable. Rising nominal interest rates globally are, and will continue to, test the resilience of the financial system and all economic participants. The financial system is complex, making it hard to pinpoint what, if any, particular 'Achilles heel' exists in real time. All we know is that the financial system has experienced many legal, operational, financial and/or reputational problems in the past - few of which were predictable in timing or scale. Most recently, for example, in the UK we saw liguidity issues rapidly escalate in their pension-investment industry as an unintended conseguence of fiscal policy announcements. Meanwhile, in other countries, IMF and World Bank financial assistance is being drawn on heavily to manage through both short-term food and energy crises, and longer- term climate change risk mitigation and adaptation. Notable also is the growing 'home bias' and 'flight to quality' being expressed by global investors as they shift their capital. Supporting these trends is the heightened geopolitical risks that exist, leading to increased fragmentation in global trading blocs and economic reliance. The rising US dollar value relative to most other currencies in the world is an important symptom of these capital movements. Aside from appearing as an investor's safe haven, the US Federal Reserve is appropriately lifting their interest rates in order to constrain consumer price inflation. US dollar deposits are now yielding more and hence attracting global capital inflows. A strong US dollar provides challenges to smaller-open economies. For example, nations with US- pegged or managed exchange rates are needing to use their foreign dollar reserves to support their currency. Those nations with floating exchange rates - such as New Zealand - are experiencing higher imported cost pressures, which can lead to longer-term embedded inflation if expectations become unanchored. There is also rising tension globally between monetary policy aimed at low and stable inflation, and governments' longer-term fiscal priorities. Governments are looking to provide necessary support to those people most impacted by geopolitical tensions (e.g. defence, food, and energy support), and health and wellbeing related expenses accentuated by the COVID pandemic - amongst many other priorities. This fiscal tension is further accentuated by the need to progress climate change adaptation. Investment is needed at scale to manage a transition to more environmentally-sustainable forms of economic production. Investment will put demand pressure on resources and hence inflation in the near-term. Likewise, there are potential one-off relative energy price changes as nations move away from fossil fuels to more sustainable alternatives. The rising geopolitical tensions are also significantly constraining global trade. This is concerning when you consider how important the decline in the relative price of technology-related goods has been in maintaining low inflation over recent decades. Less access to shared resources and technology globally will slow potential output growth - all other things equal. Sudden changes in trade access will have significant economic effects. The tensions mentioned above between: inflation and employment; rising interest rates and financial stability; monetary and long-term fiscal policy; geopolitical concerns; and climate change are already testing political consensus within and between countries. The most used word of the IMF and World Bank meetings was 'fragmentation' of global trade and policy consensus. These are some of the 'urgent' challenges facing the global economy. Just for completeness, let's not forget the 'important' challenges that existed prior to this COVID-affected business cycle. I have already briefly mentioned the critical issue of climate change adaptation. However, it is more, not less, pressing now due to the geopolitical tensions forcing energy prices up and prolonging the use of fossil fuels. In addition, most large economies - notably including China - have ageing populations. New Zealand is included in this demographic. The ratio of dependent-to-working-age population is rising rapidly. The health and fiscal costs associated with the ageing populations is significant. At the broadest brush, the youth are primarily in less developed countries and in need of significant investment in capability and capacity so as to be engaged fully in the global economy. Whether global migration will be managed or chaotic is a pressing global choice that cannot be avoided. I will finish my list of things to worry about with the obvious - the ongoing global health challenges related to COVID strains, and the ability to retain social cohesion as people compete for resources. Humanity has been truly challenged by the pandemic. We are managing, but we need to continue to collaborate. What policy options were offered up by the congregation of economic policy makers? The IMF and World Bank formula for success is best summarised in the following four key areas: Inflation needs to be contained in a 'goldilocks' manner, where tightening is sufficient to tame inflation expectations, but without sending countries into a deep recession. Fiscal policy needs to be at the least targeted and temporary. Targeted toward the people most impacted by higher food and energy prices, and temporary in that policies can be removed when the circumstances permit. Financial resilience building is critical, so that the financial system can do what it does best, allocate resources to their best long-term use. This is especially so in the rapidly growing 'non-bank' sectors of the global financial system. Ongoing structural reform is required to enhance productivity and enable the flow of resources to efficient use. It is this area of global economic policy that has received least attention for some time, with the focus being on monetary and fiscal stabilisation through the COVID years, and now war, energy constraints, and food shortages. The four steps to ongoing economic resilience are firmly within the New Zealand way of doing things. We are in relatively good stead. Next week we will be publishing our biannual Financial Stability Report, outlining our latest assessment of the soundness and efficiency of the country's financial system. I am pleased to provide a teaser in that New Zealand's financial system remains well placed to support the economy - with banks' capital and liquidity positions strong, and profitability and asset quality high. However, there will be stresses in business and amongst households as interest rates and asset prices adjust. Of critical importance to overall financial stability will be the robustness of the labour market. In regards to our monetary policy objective, we have our eyes firmly focused on meeting our inflation target. We'll be back at the end of November with our full Monetary Policy Statement and outlook ahead. Our work reviewing our monetary policy in the past five years is also near delivery. This will canvass what the Monetary Policy Committee did and why, what worked, and what we could have done better - the lessons from our experience. The work is being reviewed by independent experts and our new Board, and will be published mid-November. Finally, I want to acknowledge the important work the Financial Market Authority and our other Council of Financial Regulators partners are delivering to support the functioning of New Zealand's financial system. Our individual work plus our collective themes - climate, technology, data, and inclusion - will help ensure that New Zealand has a world-class financial system. In summary, I am confident that New Zealand is in a strong absolute and relative position to manage the challenges ahead, and that we will work together to tackle these issues. Thank you for the opportunity to join you today, it really is great to be here in person, and I hope you enjoy the rest of the conference. Meitaki ma'ata Tena koutou, tena koutou, tena koutou katoa

Title: The path back to low inflation in New Zealand
Subtitle: Chief Economist Paul Conway will give a speech on inflation at the KangaNews ANZ New Zealand Capital Markets Forum 2023.
text: The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand Delivery: 1.15pm, 23 March 2023 Venue: Intercontinental Hotel, Wellington 4 Reserve Bank xxxx of New Zealand xx Te Putea Matua Introduction Thank you for inviting me to speak today. It's a pleasure to be here, especially in person. I'm going to talk about why we are currently suffering a serious bout of inflation and what the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is doing about it. This is important not only for the Reserve Bank, but for all New Zealanders because inflation impacts all of us. According to the latest data - which is for the December quarter last year - annual consumer price inflation was 7.2%, which is around the highest it has been since the late 1980s (Figure 1). High inflation creates economic costs and distortions.1 For example, unexpected inflation makes it more difficult for people to see relative price changes in the economy, increasing the likelihood of poor decisions being made. People devote more time and effort to minimising inflation risks, rather than more productive endeavours. Even when expected, inflation still hurts. For example, when interest rates increase to compensate for the declining value of money, lenders pay tax on the additional interest and borrowers may have to cut other spending to pay higher interest bills. Overall, inflation leads to misallocated resources and lower living standards. Less wealthy and less financially sophisticated people are more likely to lose out. Keeping inflation low and stable, as was generally the case in the three decades prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, is the best contribution monetary policy can make to promoting economic wellbeing and prosperity. This is enshrined in the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act (2021) and why maintaining price stability is a fundamental part of the MPC's Remit.2 We remain deeply committed in our work of bringing inflation down and keeping it low and stable in future. Quite simply, that's our job. I want to leave you with four key messages from this speech:  Inflation is high and widespread because strong demand outstripped supply. Businesses passed on higher costs and workers sought higher pay to compensate for higher prices. Fiscal and monetary responses to the pandemic supported demand while health measures and other shocks reduced the supply of labour and products.  We are worse off because of the pandemic, the war and floods. Monetary policy cannot do anything about the loss of real income stemming from these events.  Monetary policy is lowering inflation by lifting interest rates to ensure persistence in inflation above our inflation target is squeezed out of the economy. We are incredibly determined to get inflation and inflation expectations back to target.  Returning inflation to target could be made more difficult if businesses and workers try to push up their real profit margins and real wages to make up for the inflationary impact of the 1 See, for example, Samantha Johnson (1993) "The costs of inflation revisited", Reserve Bank Bulletin, Vol 56, No 1. Pp 3-31. 2 Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021 (legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2021/0031/latest/LMS286978.html) and Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Replacement of Remit for Monetary Policy Committee) Order 2021 Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Replacement of Remit for Monetary Policy Committee) Order 2021 (LI 2021/29) Contents - New Zealand Legislation. 2 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand pandemic, the war, and the storms. In this case, Monetary Policy would need to be more contractionary for longer, resulting in a deeper recession. Figure 1: Annual CPI inflation in New Zealand % Source: Stats NZ, RBNZ estimates. Note: Shaded bar represents the inflation target range since the introduction of inflation targeting in 1989. From 2012, a focus on the 2 per cent target midpoint was added (blue line). How Did We Get High Inflation? Reduced Ability to Produce Goods and Services The COVID-19 pandemic and war and related events reduced the ability of the global economy to produce goods and services. Global supply chains were severely disrupted, especially for us living here in the South Pacific - the last bus stop on the planet. This really was a severe "black swan event" for global logistics. Labour shortages have also been incredibly intense globally and in New Zealand. As COVID-19 spread, a large share of the global workforce was sick or isolating and couldn't work. For example, in March 2022, the number of people off work in New Zealand for a week or more because of sickness was up almost 70% compared with a year earlier.3 It is not just the health impacts of COVID-19 that led to worker shortages. In some countries, the pandemic caused people to reassess their priorities and, in many cases, to stop working for a time or retire early. We didn't see so much of this in New Zealand, where participation in the labour market remained incredibly strong and is currently at record highs. But when our border dosed in the early days of the pandemic, international arrivals and departures collapsed to near zero. Net migration then 3 "More people away from work due to sickness" - Stats NZ (stats.govt.nz/news/more-people-away-from-work-due-to-sickness/). 3 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand turned negative through 2020 and 2021 as permanent or long term departures increased while arrivals stayed low. This was in stark contrast to previous years of very large migration inflows. Our labour market tightened. Over mid-2020, suggestive of structural change in the economy, unemployment and job vacancies both increased (Figure 2). But from the end of 2020, unemployment fell and job vacancies increased further as workers became increasingly difficult to find. The share of people moving between jobs also increased strongly, as competition for workers increased (Figure 3). As borders re-opened, younger New Zealanders have been leaving, further reducing the domestic pool of workers. The labour market has remained incredibly tight, with high vacancy rates and low unemployment. The recent summer flooding in Auckland and Cyclone Gabrielle have also reduced supply in some industries. You will have no doubt experienced the results of supply chain disruptions and worker shortages over recent years: for example, shops being closed because of staff illness; long waits for online purchases as international and domestic supply chains came under pressure; high food price inflation, and high petrol prices when the war in Ukraine impacted energy markets. Unemployment rate (%) Source: Stats NZ, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (M Bl E), RBNZ estimates. Note: The vacancy rate is defined as the number of job vacancies as a share of the labour force. Colours reflect different periods in recent history. Pink: COVID-19 (2020-2022); Black: post-GFC (2009Q3-2019); Orange: GFC (2008-2009Q2); blue: pre-GFC (1990-2007). 4 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand Figure 3: Job-to-job transitions % of potential GDP % of WAP Source: Stats NZz Stats NZ IDI, RBNZ estimates. Note: WAP stands for 'working-age population'. Private sector job-to-job transitions exclude transitions in the Education and Training and Public Administration and Safety industries. Job-to-job transitions data points for December 2017 and March 2018 have been removed due to data guality concerns. Resilient Demand and Spending While the supply of goods and services was restricted, spending and demand in the economy remained strong. Quite simply, demand outstripped our ability to supply. For us in New Zealand, this partly reflected the effectiveness of our health response to COVID-19. While lockdowns were tough going - especially for people living in Auckland - economic life for many New Zealanders was surprisingly 'normal' for many months during the global pandemic. At the same time, Government support to the economy increased over 2020. New packages, such as the Wage Subsidy Scheme, were designed and rolled out at pace. Interest rates were pushed lower, with the Official Cash Rate (OCR) dropped to its 'effective lower bound' and additional monetary policy tools put in place. For the most part, people remained in work, which supported income growth. There were also large build-ups of cash balances and savings, given limited spending opportunities during lockdowns. This also supported household spending and demand in the economy as restrictions were gradually eased. Demand has been resilient overall, but there have been big swings in what people have been spending their money on, given changing consumer preferences and economic realities. Perhaps most obviously, as borders around the world closed, a precipitous drop in visitor arrivals hit tourism spending hard. More generally, spending requiring face-to-face contact - mostly in service industries such as cafes, bars, and shops - fell sharply as the pandemic hit. On the flip side, spending on goods that could be bought online and delivered surged. The online economy grew strongly over this period. 5 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand Construction also boomed as resilient incomes, low unemployment, and low interest rates increased demand for housing. People spending more time at home - either working from home or locked down - also increased housing demand. With constraints on housing supply, stronger demand contributed to a 44% increase in house prices from early 2020 to late 2021 4 Unusually, given we were in the middle of a global pandemic, household wealth increased, adding to spending pressures via a wealth effect. That is, people tend to spend more when their wealth increases. More recently, as health restrictions were progressively removed, demand for services has increased strongly, particularly in hospitality and tourism. Demand for used cars and other products destroyed in the cyclone has also spiked. So, over the last few years, the story has been one of resilient demand but with big swings and changes in its composition. Resilient Demand at a Time of Disrupted and Limited Supply Causes Inflation Resilient demand plus supply-side issues eguals inflation. To start with, bottlenecks led to sharp price increases for specific products. Perhaps the most obvious example was when supply restrictions caused by the war in Ukraine sent global energy and food prices sharply higher. As a small open economy, it was impossible for New Zealand to avoid inflationary pressures caused by global events. Almost half of headline inflation in New Zealand over the pandemic originated offshore (Figure 4). Keeping headline inflation in the 1-3% target over this time would have required monetary policy to be highly contractionary to reduce home-grown (non-tradable) inflation, in order to offset imported inflationary pressure. Excess demand dynamics also played out in some domestic markets. For instance, construction and housing-related costs are less influenced by global events but have risen sharply over the past two years because of difficulties finding materials (such as Gib plasterboard) and workers. Inflation in the tourism industry is another example. Tourism is on the front line of labour shortages and still rebuilding capacity lost during the early years of the pandemic. With higher demand driven by a rapid rebound in international visitors, prices charged by many tourism- related businesses have increased sharply. 4 Housing (Still) Matters - The Big Picture rbnz.govt.nz/hub/publications/speech/2022/speech2022-06-30 6 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand Big swings in the composition of demand may also be inflationary. Recent work from the Bank of England finds that prices don't fall much in industries hit with weaker demand but increase quickly in industries facing into stronger demand.5 This asymmetric response might explain why overall inflation did not fall in 2020 but increased strongly as demand started rebounding. Figure 4: Tradable inflation as a share of headline inflation % Source: Stats NZ Inflation Becomes Widespread and Persistent In 2021, inflation increased mainly because of a relatively small number of large price increases, suggesting excess demand for a few specific products (Figure 5). In 2022, small price increases across a large number of products contributed to inflation, suggesting widespread inflation pressures in the economy. Inflation can become widespread in a number of ways. Price increases may spread through the economy as businesses try to pass on higher input costs and workers try to maintain the spending power of their incomes by seeking higher pay. With a very tight labour market and weak competition in some parts of our economy, the scope for price increases to become embedded in cost-price dynamics and trigger second-round inflationary effects is high. These second-round effects create ongoing inflation, even after the original stimulus - a relative price shock for specific products like petrol or plasterboard - has died away. Inflation can also spread through the economy because it is easier for firms to increase prices when other firms are doing likewise. Customers may think it more reasonable that firms increase their prices when there is inflation in the economy. Inflation can become persistent if people expect it to stay high in future. If people make decisions today based on the expectation of higher prices in future, then inflation will persist. Inflation 5 Bunn, P., Anayi, L. S., Bloom, N., Mizen, P., Thwaites, G., & Yotzov, I. (2022). Firming up price inflation (No. w30505). National Bureau of Economic Research. 7 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand expectations can become self-fulfilling in that once inflation starts, the belief that it will continue can sustain it. Figure 5: The distribution of price changes % 35 Annual price change range (%) Source: RBNZ calculations using Statistics New Zealand CPI level 3 class data, INFOS CPI013AA, containing price indices for 109 categories (e.g. Bread and cereals; Women's clothing; Postal services). Note: The graphs show the distribution of annual price increases each year, calculated as the fraction of items which have a price increase in 2 percentage point intervals eg 0 - 2%, 2 - 4%. The fractions are calculated using contemporaneous CPI weights. For example, between 2001 and 2020, 31% of categories had price increases between 2 and 4%, on average; this fraction fell to 28% in 2021 and 14% in 2022. The graph shows that in 2021 there was only a small reduction in the number of categories having price increases of 4% or less, but a large increase in the number of categories having very large price increases, particularly price increases above 30%. In contrast, in 2022 there was a rightward shift of the whole distribution, with a large reduction in the number of categories with less than 4% price increases, and a large increase in the number price increases between 4 and 12%. How to Tame Inflation What Monetary Policy Can't Do Before outlining how MPC is working to lower inflation, I want to briefly touch on what monetary policy can't do. Monetary policy can't do anything about income lost because of the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and recent natural disasters. These losses reflect a reduced ability to produce goods and services. While monetary policy can and must respond to inflationary pressures caused by excess demand, it cannot do much to improve the ability of our economy to produce output. For example, the Reserve Bank can do nothing to make up for a shortage of kumara or onions or apples caused by flooding. Instead, improving productivity is the best way to lift incomes sustainably. By alleviating supply constraints, better productivity would also reduce long-run inflationary pressures at minimal economic cost. More productive businesses can hold or even cut prices while paying workers more and remaining competitive. 8 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand True, lifting productivity has not been easy in New Zealand, which is why New Zealanders work more hours than most in the developed world but earn relatively low incomes. One reason for our poor productivity is that competition may be weak in some New Zealand markets, making it easier for businesses to pass on cost increases to their customers. Improving competition is about regulatory changes that lower barriers to entry and discourage anti-competitive behaviours. It is excellent to see the Commerce Commission now doing Market Studies and having better regulatory tools at its disposal to pursue abuse of dominance cases. There are also things people can do to enhance the power of competition and keep price pressures in check. Shop around for that good deal. Wait for the sales. Use price comparison websites. And go to the effort of changing banks or utility providers if it means getting a better deal. How MPC is Working to Lower Inflation While higher productivity and more competitive markets are essential for lifting our economic performance and blunting inflationary pressures over the long run, the responsibility for reducing current inflation back into the 1-3% target band sits firmly with MPC. With inflation above 7% and far outside the target range, MPC has been increasing the OCR to bring demand back into balance with the supply capacity of our economy. Ideally, and with the benefit of hindsight, monetary policy should have started tightening earlier in 2021. This, along with many other lessons learned, was recognised by the Reserve Bank in our recent review of monetary policy over the past five years.6 In any case, at 4.75%, the OCR has increased by 450 basis points in only 18 months. In nominal terms, this is the most rapid increase in its history and the highest it has been since before the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. Higher Interest Rates Soften Demand and Lower Inflation In short, monetary policy shifts demand in the economy through time. Higher interest rates reduce demand by encouraging people to spend less and save more while lower interest rates have the opposite effect. Higher interest rates push economic activity into the future whereas lower interest rates pull activity into the present. 6 In retrospect: Monetary policy in New Zealand 2017 to 2022 - rbnz.govt.nz/hub/publications/monetary-policy-statement/rafimp. 9 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand So, as we work to rein in inflation, mortgage-holders and businesses looking for finance are seeing their interest rates increasing. People with savings are seeing the nominal return on their savings increase. However, the after-tax real return on savings may still be negative, given high inflation, sluggish increases in terms deposit rates, and tax settings. But over time, higher interest rates will encourage saving and restrict spending by households with mortgages. They will also hold back hiring decisions, and may lead to lower cash flow and lower asset prices, as we have already seen with house prices. Less helpfully, higher interest rates may also restrict business investment. All that will help lower aggregate demand in the economy. In turn, this will mean less excess demand in product and labour markets, which will mean lower inflation and employment moving back towards its maximum sustainable level. As in many countries around the world, we expect this monetary policy tightening to cause the New Zealand economy to enter a mild recession later this year as demand slows. Expectations Really Matter The effectiveness of higher interest rates in bringing balance to the economy and lowering inflation depends on how realistic and pragmatic New Zealanders are in accepting that we are worse off than we otherwise would be given global events of the past few years and recent storms. As Governor Adrian Orr puts it, the people of planet earth are poorer because of the pandemic and war. The recent floods in Auckland and the cyclone along the East Coast have also reduced wealth and prosperity in New Zealand. In practice, this means accepting the fact of higher prices for some producer inputs and consumption goods, meaning lower real wages and profits than otherwise. If businesses and workers try to push their real profit margins and real wages to where they would have been if not for the pandemic, the war, and storms, then the more likely it is that high inflationary pressures persist into the future. Resisting the squeeze on real incomes and spending power would mean MPC has to increase interest rates further or hold them up for longer, and the deeper any recession would need to be to get inflation back within the target band. As I outlined earlier, monetary policy cannot do anything about the loss of real income stemming from global events and natural disasters. What we can and are doing is lifting interest rates to ensure any self-sustaining persistence in inflation above the inflation target is squeezed out of the economy by constraining demand relative to supply as necessary. By the same token, if businesses and households make decisions today based on the expectation of rising prices in future, then inflationary pressures will persist. Higher interest rates for longer and a deeper recession would again be necessary to bring inflation back to target. Conversely, if people expect inflation to be within the 1-3% target in future and act accordingly, the less work we have to do with higher interest rates that weaken demand. 10 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand Taming inflation means ensuring that short-term inflation expectations do not just reflect current high inflation and that medium-term inflation expectations do not drift so that long-term expectations remain anchored to the inflation target (Figure 6). The path back from persistent to low inflation always involves some output losses and lower incomes overall. The size of those losses depends on how realistic we all are in adjusting to new economic realities and in expecting inflation to fall back to target, consistent with MPC's Remit. Figure 6: Inflation expectations % 6 0 -------------- 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 Source: RBNZ Survey of Expectations (Business). Monetary Policymaking in a World of Change If that didn't already sound complicated, let me layer on some of the complexities and uncertainties MPC faces when making interest rate decisions. (And can I stress that decisions on the OCR are reached through consensus by the seven members of MPC.) First, the global economy is highly volatile, fragile, and uncertain. Economic growth rates have been slowing, partly in response to higher interest rates, and international organisations paint a gloomy future for the global economy. Globalisation is changing, with big implications for small economies such as ours. The global trading system is fracturing along political lines and geopolitical tensions are rife. The transition to net zero carbon emissions will lead to further changes in the global balance of power and trade relations. This presents MPC with a very volatile and challenging international environment to navigate over the current cycle. It also raises big questions about the type of economy we will face once inflation is back within the target band. 11 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand On the domestic front, our hearts go out to people impacted by the recent storms and floods in the North Island. The material and financial losses are clearly substantial. With no spare capacity in the economy, diverting resources into cyclone-affected areas for the rebuild will mean reducing activity in other parts of the country. There are a number of ways this rebalancing could occur, each with different implications for interest rate. If the rebuild generates inflationary pressure, interest rates would increase, reducing demand and freeing up resources for the rebuild. Alternatively, diverting Government resources from projects elsewhere in the country or funding the rebuild via increased government revenues would free up resources without the need for higher interest rates. Another uncertainty growing increasingly pertinent as we near the interest rate peak is knowing when monetary policy has done enough to get inflation comfortably back to target. The effects of the 450 basis point increase in the OCR over the last 18 months are still percolating through the economy. For instance, over the coming year, 50% of mortgages will roll off low fixed- term rates onto much higher rates. The 'average' mortgage rate will move from 4.5% to over 6%. We assume this will affect consumer spending in a similar way to interest rate increases in previous cycles. But the rapid speed of rate increases creates additional uncertainty about how the effects of the tightening will play out. It is also unclear whether inflation expectations are falling fast enough to mean current and projected OCR settings are consistent with positive real interest rates, and thus likely to be disinflationary. In part, this comes down to how convinced people are that MPC will do what's necessary to get inflation down. On balance, our measures of neutral interest rates - the interest rate that is neither stimulatory nor contractionary - indicate the OCR is now comfortably above neutral and having the desired contractionary effect. Consistent with this, and as discussed in detail in the February Monetary Policy Statement, there are welcome signs demand in the economy is slowing. Achieving the Remit Monetary policy is not just about returning inflation to target and keeping it there. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act (2021) instructs us to also support maximum sustainable employment. Currently, with inflation well above target and employment clearly above its maximum sustainable level, achieving this dual mandate requires contractionary monetary policy to slow domestic spending and employment and to lower inflation. However, in a stagflation environment of low growth, rising unemployment and high inflation, the optimal path for interest rates becomes less clear. Would MPC raise interest rates to control inflation or lower rates to encourage growth and jobs? In this situation, history and economic theory suggest a policy response aimed at a more drawn- out return of inflation to target and a smaller decline in employment. But if inflation expectations move higher, the optimal response is to put greater weight on returning inflation to target. This would support maximum sustainable employment in the medium 12 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand term by reducing the need for an extended period of contractionary monetary policy to get even higher inflation expectations back to target. Our Monetary Policy Remit also instructs us to have regard to the efficiency and soundness of the financial system and to avoid unnecessary instability in output, interest rates, and the exchange rate. We also have to discount transitory inflationary events and assess the impact of MPC decisions on the Government's policy on house prices. In practice, this means we have a medium term focus for our price stability objective. The flexibility that allows us is important in that it ensures we can maintain price stability over time without causing unnecessary damage to the economy. We are currently reviewing our Remit and will give advice to the Minister of Finance in April. Conclusion The title of this speech is how to get back to low inflation in New Zealand. In a narrow sense, this is about getting monetary policy right so inflation returns to target. This means firms, workers and taxpayers accepting the distributional consequences of recent global and domestic shocks and lowering their inflation expectations accordingly. We are well placed to cope with this adjustment. The economy has grown strongly over the pandemic and unemployment and headline CPI are both in the lower third of OCED economies, while core inflation is about middle of the pack. Household balance sheets are in good shape in aggregate and the banking system is very well capitalised, meaning there is no conflict between monetary policy and financial stability. In a broader sense, getting monetary policy right in a complex and volatile environment means building a deep understanding of the evolving economic context in which monetary policy operates. This requires an ambitious economic research agenda, including the use of new and improved data for monitoring and understanding the economy. It also requires strong collaboration across the public sector and with the domestic and international academic community. For example, we must work with the Treasury to understand the future role of fiscal policy instruments in managing economic shocks. In the broadest sense, getting back to low inflation is about improving the ability of the New Zealand economy to thrive in a rapidly evolving global environment. But that's a conversation for another day. 13 The Path Back to Low Inflation in New Zealand

Title: Informed investment decisions support financial system stability
text: Informed investment decisions support financial system stability Comments delivered to New Zealand - OECD International Network on Financial Education in Auckland On 10-14 October 2016 By Grant Spencer, Deputy Governor 2 The Terrace, PO Box 2498, Wellington 6140, New Zealand Telephone 64 4 472 2029 Online at Introduction I join Andre Laboule and Diane Maxwell in welcoming you all to this meeting of the OECD International Network on Financial Education (INFE), and may I also welcome you to New Zealand. I know most of you have travelled long distances to attend the meetings this week. I hope you find your stay in Auckland productive and enjoyable. I offer particular thanks to our joint host, Diane Maxwell and the New Zealand Commission for Financial Capability, for inviting me to your meeting today and for putting together an impressive program of meetings and activities over this week. As a founding member, the Commission has made a strong contribution to the INFE since its inception in 2008. While not a member of the INFE, I certainly have a close interest in the network and its work. I chair the OECD Financial Markets Committee (CMF) which is one of the two OECD committees that oversee the work of the INFE. We take particular interest in the work around measurement and policy development that is mandated by the G20. A current issue of interest is the influence of new digital technology on financial education and financial inclusion. A session of our upcoming CMF meeting in Paris will be devoted to the potential implications of new Fintech developments across a number of fronts, including as a financial education tool. The role of new technology in shaping financial behaviour is also relevant to me in my main job as Head of financial Stability at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. The Bank is not responsible for investor protection, which is the role of the New Zealand Financial Markets Authority (FMA). Rather we are responsible for prudential regulation and the overall stability of the New Zealand financial system. Nevertheless, a well informed and educated investing public is crucially important for the safety of the overall financial system as well as for the welfare of the investing public. I would like to take a few minutes to expand on this theme and to describe some recent developments where we are using technology to improve the quality of bank disclosure, with the ultimate aim of a more informed and resilient banking system. Three pillars approach to supervision The Banks approach to promoting financial system stability is based on the three pillars of market discipline, self-discipline and regulatory discipline. We have strengthened our regulatory discipline 5051664 3 pillar in recent years, but still have a less intensive approach to supervision than other international regulators. We do not, for example, conduct on-site supervision of the entities we regulate. Our main focus is on market and self-discipline. The self-discipline regime focuses on the responsibility of boards and senior management to ensure sound risk management practices through their organisations. For market discipline, two important elements are disclosure and the absence of deposit insurance. The Reserve Bank was an early pioneer in disclosure and it continues to be a key element in our regime. Banks and finance companies must disclose information that allows investors to make informed choices about where to put their money, in particular to understand the risks as well as the returns inherent in investment choices. The absence of deposit insurance in New Zealand means that investors can lose money if a New Zealand financial institution fails. This underpins market discipline as investors are incentivised to be vigilant and make informed investment choices. This helps to promote a healthier and safer financial system. The Reserve Bank and the New Zealand Government believe deposit insurance blunts incentives for both financial institutions and depositors to monitor and manage risks properly. Disclosure and education Proper disclosure by financial institutions and market discipline clearly work best in an environment where everyone is financially educated. It is in peoples own interests and in societys interest, that investors understand at least the basics of risk and return. Such understanding  based on education and information - certainly helps the Reserve Bank to achieve its system stability objective. All investors, from individuals saving for a house deposit to professional fund managers, need to understand the risks involved, for example:  In the current stretched housing market  what could happen to me financially if the market turned down? And how much debt can I really afford?  In todays world of low interest rates, if I go for a higher interest investment, or shares, what risks am I really taking on?  How can I protect the value of my retirement nest egg without taking undue risks? Investors and their advisors need accurate and relevant information in order to answer such questions and to make sensible decisions about where to put their money. 5051664 4 Role of Technology Looking forward, there is no doubt the transparency of investments can be enhanced by modern technology. Todays technology can be used to generate more timely, comparable and accessible information on investment alternatives. The Reserve Bank is currently undertaking public consultation on a proposed Dashboard approach to public disclosure by banks. The Dashboard would provide a side-by-side comparison of the banks financial health, located on the Reserve Banks website and updated quarterly. This would supplement the more extensive but less comparable disclosure statements that banks currently prepare. The aim of the Dashboard would be to help investors with more timely and comparable information on banks, so that all investors can make better decisions about where to put their money. Technology offers a huge range of opportunities for financial education, particularly in making information more accessible and more user-friendly. In New Zealand, an important recent example of this is the work that the Commission for Financial Capability have done to provide information about alternative KiwiSaver products on their Sorted website /. The Reserve Bank sees its Dashboard very much in the same vein. As a web-based tool, a major advantage of the Dashboard will be the ability to track its usage. This will help to assess the Dashboards usefulness over time and allow us to regularly improve its content and structure to ensure it is achieving its purpose. Technology is giving us new and more dynamic ways of achieving this. Role of regulation and tax Transparency and a healthy financial system are supported by regulatory and tax frameworks that do not favour one investment over another and which facilitate the development of new financial products. The regulatory framework should also ensure that financial advisers are incentivised to look after their clients interests, not their own. Recent changes to the Financial Markets Conduct Act have resulted in changes to the way financial products are offered and promoted. These frameworks play a key role in building confidence in our markets and providing a level playing field for investors. Conclusion Disclosure, technology and regulation are very important but can get us only so far. Society has a responsibility to give individuals at least a basic knowledge of financial risk and return. Financial regulators have a responsibility to provide the incentives and information that allow people to use 5051664 5 that knowledge in making investment decisions. Educated investors, transparency of financial providers and advice geared to the needs of investors will all help to deliver fewer financial crises, higher quality investments and a stable financial system. I wish you well for a productive meeting today which will see the discussion and approval of the program of work for the next biennium. And I am sure you will have a very successful Symposium tomorrow. 5051664

Title: Another seismic shift in New Zealand banking regulatory reform
Subtitle: RBNZ Director of Enforcement and Resolution Kerry Beaumont will give a speech about the evolution of prudential regulation and supervision of banks in New Zealand at the 39th Annual Conference of the Banking and Financial Services Law Association.
text: UNCLASSIFIED (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 A speech delivered to the Banking and Financial Services Law Association Conference in Queenstown 4 September 2023 By Kerry Beaumont, Director of Enforcement & Resolution, Te Putea Matua, Reserve Bank of New Zealand Reserve Bank of New Zealand xx Te Putea Matua UNCLASSIFIED Introduction Today we are going to take you on a journey through the life and times of the Deposit Takers Act ('DTA') 2023. We will cover the key bones of the DTA, how it differs from its predecessor legislation and what industry can expect in terms of how we now go about bringing the DTA into full force. Prudential regulation in New Zealand - a short history The beginning Central banks emerged from the strongest financial institution acting as the banker to the government and to the banks, and as lender of last resort. This history goes back to Sweden's Riksbank (established 1668), the Bank of England (established 1694), the United States' Federal Reserve (established 1913) and, for New Zealand, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand - Te Putea Matua (established 1934)12. This position at the heart of the financial system made central banks the natural institution to also take a public policy role, with responsibility for the stability of the financial system. Indeed, monetary and financial stability are in many ways intrinsically linked, as both functions seek to achieve broader economic stability.
