They are different sides of the same coin and there is a complementarity between the two: a stable financial system is a precondition for the effective transmission of monetary policy (via the banking system), and price stability can also be regarded as a precondition for financial stability.1 * 3 In New Zealand, the first formal responsibility for prudential regulation and supervision of banks was provided for in the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Amendment Act 1986.4 The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 (the '1989 Act')5 carried over this responsibility, with the purpose of promoting the maintenance of a sound and efficient financial system' (section 68(a)).6 These changes were part of the New Zealand financial reforms of the 1980s, which included privatisation of the Government-owned bank and liberalisation of financial markets. 1 For more information on the evolution of central banking, readers may be interested in the following publication on The World Bank's website: 'The evolution of central banking' author Capie, Forest, dated 30 November 1995: Source: - of-central-banking. For more information on the evolution of central banking, readers may be interested in the following publication on The World Bank's website: 'The evolution of central banking' author Capie, Forest, dated 30 November 1995: Source: - of-central-banking. 3 For more information on how money and financial stability are linked, readers may be interested the following speech from the Executive Director of Financial Stability at the Bank of England, Sarah Breeden: 4 The Amendment Act provided for application for registration as banks by interested parties of sound financial condition and with expertise in banking. It also gave the Reserve Bank extended powers to monitor the financial condition and risk exposure of banks as part of its prudential supervision, and in some circumstances to manage the exit from financial markets of failing institutions. The Act was passed into law on 24 December 1986, with effect from 1 April 1987. Source: /- /media/483e545d5e1c4940a80cb23966655bd7.ashx?sc_langen 5 This Act is now formally known as the Banking (Prudential Supervision) Act 1989. This change came into effect under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021. 6 The 1989 Act formalised the essential elements of monetary policy as it had been practised since 1985, with the main change aimed at improving the transparency and consistency of monetary policy. In particular, the Act put in place a statutory commitment to achieving price stability as well as providing an environment in which the right incentives exist for this to be accomplished. (Under the old legislation monetary policy could be aimed at several sometimes conflicting objectives. In addition, the Bank could be directed by the Minister of Finance to follow a particular policy without that directive being released publicly.) Source: 1 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED Following these reforms, throughout the 1990s and until recently, the Reserve Bank was well known internationally for its 'light handed' approach to prudential supervision. This involved an emphasis on self and market discipline, together with comparatively conservative regulatory settings in a small number of prudential policy areas. The light-handed approach manifested itself by having a small supervisory department at the Reserve Bank, limited direct monitoring of banks by supervisors, and no prudential on-site inspections of banks. The latter was a distinguishing feature of our approach. Most regulators around the world use on-site inspections as a standard tool of their supervisory approach to validate or verify prudential information provided by entities. The Reserve Bank, however, did have the power to appoint external experts to carry out in-depth investigations. Market discipline was pursued through, among other incentives, extensive quarterly public disclosure rules introduced in 1996. The absence of deposit protection was also one of the distinguishing features of this approach - the fear of moral hazard. This approach was designed to provide depositors with a strong incentive to monitor the financial strength of their bank, and force riskier banks to pay more for their funding, thus incentivising them to act more prudently. Self-discipline relied on governance requirements that compelled directors to act in the best interests of the New Zealand bank. Notably, incorrect director attestations could lead to penalties such as imprisonment. This approach was meant to align incentives on banks' boards with the sound management of banks. On the other hand, the Reserve Bank's regulatory framework comprised a very conservative approach to capital settings, in of terms of both the amount that banks needed to have, and the quality of that capital, i.e., an emphasis on common equity ('CETT). This was further buttressed by comparatively strict governance, disclosure, and local incorporation requirements (as well as the adoption of the Basel II Capital Framework, issued by the Basel Committee). The Reserve Bank was also leading in developing its open bank resolution policy (OBR) (an early form of 'bail-in') and its liquidity policy. The latter predates equivalent Basel Committee settings. While many would say this approach served New Zealand well, it was also not without its criticism. For example:  The reliance on market discipline, particularly when it comes to depositors being able to exercise it, had always received its fair share of scrutiny.  There was scepticism whether depositors were sufficiently aware of the role they had been given or indeed had the financial capability to exercise market discipline.  Others argued that the reliance on market discipline and absence of some form of depositor protection or compensation would not withstand a real crisis. Moreover, New Zealand became increasingly an outlier by international comparison at a time when there was a move closer to regulatory orthodoxy, partly due to the extraterritorial reach of international legislation and the benefits of equivalence treatments. 2 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED Late 2000's - the start of the shift The shift in the underlying philosophy started around the time of and following the global financial crisis ('the GFC') in 2008. The Government put in place the Crown Retail Deposit Guarantee Scheme to provide retail depositor confidence in New Zealand and, to ostensibly avoid a flight of funds from New Zealand institutions to those in Australia. This was in part a response to the introduction of the Australian guarantee scheme at the same time. Nine finance companies in the Scheme failed, causing the Crown to pay out about 2 billion to depositors at the time. However, as recognised in the Auditor-General's performance and audit report [ojverall, the Scheme achieved its goal. No banks in New Zealand failed, and there was no run on banks. Many of the other finance institutions also survived the global financial crisis. The economy was stabilised.'7 In policy terms, the Scheme was significant. It represented the first material departure from the longstanding settings in New Zealand of minimal state intervention in the market, at least in the post-financial liberalisation era. Also in 2008, Parliament passed amendments to the 1989 Act to make the Reserve Bank the prudential regulatory authority for non-bank deposit takers ('NBDTs'). This law change followed a 2005 review by the Government of the regulatory framework of non-bank financial institutions that concluded that reforms were needed to address weaknesses in the system that could potentially undermine public confidence. This prudential regime is now contained in the Non-Bank Deposit Takers Act 2013. Very briefly, under that regime an NBDT is a person, other than a registered bank, that makes regulated offers of debt securities and carries on the business of borrowing and lending money, or providing financial services, or both.8 The NBDT Act and its regulations remains in place today and will be repealed by the DTA once the relevant provisions come into force. For completeness, I should add that 1989 Act also remains in place today. Again, until the relevant parts of the DTA come into force, the 1989 Act will continue to be the law for the prudential regulation of registered banks in New Zealand. Unlike the regime for NBDTs, a registered bank is not tied to the activity of 'banking' per se, but the ability to use the term 'bank' and its derivatives. 2016 to 2017 - International Monetary Fund assessment Over the course of 2016, New Zealand's regulatory frameworks for financial sector regulation was subject to an external audit in the form of the International Monetary Fund ('IMF')'s Financial Sector Assessment Programme (known as the 'FSAP').9 The IMF benchmarked this assessment against the principles or standards from several international standard setting bodies such as the Basel Committee. 7 'Performance audit report: The Treasury: Implementing and managing the Crown Retail Deposit Guarantee Scheme' dated September 2011 carried out under section 16 of the Public Audit Act 2001 by the Controller and Auditor-General. 3 See section 5 of the NBDT Act for further details. 9 The full report entitled 'New Zealand: Financial Sector Assessment Program: Financial System Stability Assessment' is dated 8 May 2017, and is published on the IMF website: . 3 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED With respect to banking regulation, the IMF concluded that the Reserve Bank rulebook and supervisory approach was light-handed, relative to international standards. It encouraged the Reserve Bank to issue enforceable supervisory standards on key risks, review the enforcement regime to promote preventive action, and initiate on-site programs targeted on areas of high risk. The IMF also recommended that a long-standing gap in New Zealand's financial system safety net - the absence of a formal scheme to protect depositors from loss - be addressed. The IMF's analysis was a key input into the development of the terms of reference for the later review of the 1989 Act. Over the subsequent policy development process, the FSAP formed an integral part of the problem definition underpinning various policy proposals, as well as advice to the Minister of Finance and recommendations to Cabinet. Indeed, the DTA shifts New Zealand towards the international norms for banking regulation set by the Basel Committee, by directly addressing most of the (primary legislation) relevant recommendations from the IMF. Once the Act is in full force and embedded, we would expect a more favourable assessment from the IMF in terms of compliance or alignment with the Basel core principles. A quick word on the other 'twin peak' - conduct regulation over this period To provide context, (especially for any Australian colleagues in the audience and the future leaders among us who may not have experienced this history first hand) this approach to prudential regulation and supervision, while out of step internationally, was not out of step with the previous approach and subsequent shift in New Zealand's other key pieces of financial services legislation. In the conduct space, at the extreme, the now repealed Securities Act 1978 and Securities Markets Act 1988 could also be described as light handed regimes, compared to where we are at today. We now have the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (the 'FMC Act'), which has been the subject of some excellent BFLSA presentations in past years. The FMC Act - which replaced the Securities Act and Securities Markets Act - is now the centrepiece of more rigorous conduct regulation in New Zealand. The Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008, the financial advisers regime, climate related disclosure regime and the conduct of financial institutions licensing regime all now exist to strengthen New Zealand's financial services safety nets and to better reflect international best practice. It is obvious that we are now well into in a new era of financial services regulation in New Zealand. There has been a seismic shift. With that brief history. We will now focus on the DTA itself. 4 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED 2017 to 2021 - The Review In 2017 the Government determined that while the 1989 Act has generally served New Zealanders well, the time was right for a review, as there have been significant changes to the global and New Zealand economy since 1989. Review of the 1989 Act Reserve Bark Acl Review Phase 1 Ecanormct object* Monetary policy remrt Monetary policy ccnimtte* Rmrrvc Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Act  I Governance and decision making I Ftnarcial stsbftty objective 1 Actourtability and transparency I Regulatory coordination and cooperation _ x Consultation 1 Rescrvr Bank Act X__. ...  . ' , 2 ana consultation Rrvrew Pn.Tsr 2 / j Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act (2021) Consultation 3 / Deposit Takers Bill Regulation o* banks and other deposit lakers Crisis manaixerx and resoMlon Depositor compensation UNCLASSIFIED The goal of the review was to modernise New Zealand's monetary policy and financial stability policy frameworks and the Reserve Bank's governance and accountability settings.10 The Review was undertaken in two parts, the first focussing on the monetary policy aspects of the 1989 Act, and a second on financial policy. Phase 1 of the Review was led by the Treasury, while Phase 2 was undertaken jointly by the Treasury and the Reserve Bank and was largely completed in 2021 with key policy decisions from Cabinet and the development of an exposure draft of the Bill by the Parliamentary Counsel Office. An Independent Expert Advisory Panel advised on key issues in both phases to support the work of the Review team and the joint agency steering committee. A brief overview of the outputs of the Review - New Zealand's other 'epic trilogy' is as follows: Monetary Policy Phase 1 of the Review reformed the Reserve Bank's monetary policy settings. Those changes came into force on 1 April 2019 under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Act 2018. The Reserve Bank now has a dual monetary policy mandate - price stability and contributing to maximum sustainable employment. The monetary policy remit-which replaced the earlier policy targets agreement - provides the Reserve Bank with its specific inflation target ______________ 10 Terms of Reference for the Review of the Reserve Bank Act - 2017 (Source: ') 5 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED and direction on how to consider its contribution to maximum sustainable employment.11 Phase 1 also placed the responsibility for formulating monetary policy with the Monetary Policy Committee, replacing the 'single decision-maker model' (under which the Governor was singularly responsible and accountable), and thereby bringing New Zealand into line with monetary policy governance arrangements globally. Institutional and accountability settings The first part of Phase 2 focused on the Reserve Bank's institutional and accountability settings. The outcome of this work was the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021 (the '2021 Act'), which came into full force on 1 July 2022. The 2021 Act modernised the institutional arrangements of the Reserve Bank by replacing the 'single decision maker model' with a governance board and strengthening reporting and accountability requirements. The board of the Reserve Bank is now tasked with all the responsibilities of the Reserve Bank (other than those given to the Monetary Policy Committee). Previously, the board was an agent of the Minister of Finance whose role was to monitor the performance of the Governor and the Bank more generally. That monitoring role is now assigned to the Treasury. The overarching purpose of the 2021 Act is to: promote the prosperity and well-being of New Zealanders and contribute to a sustainable and productive economy (section 3(b)) It also reframed and clarified the financial policy objective for the Reserve Bank (and provided for a financial policy remit to be issued by the Minister of Finance (section 203)).12 The Reserve Bank now has a financial policy objective of: protecting and promoting the stability of New Zealand's financial system (section 9(1)(b)) This reframing of the Reserve Bank's financial policy objective from 'soundness and efficiency' to 'financial stability' provides a clearer and more focussed prudential mandate. Soundness now appears as an additional main purpose under the DTA, while efficiency appears in the DTA's decision-making principles. Efficiency also appears in the current financial policy remit, issued by the Minister of Finance on 30 June 2022. Further information on the Reserve Bank's monetary policy settings and institutional and accountability settings can be found on our website. Prudential regulation and supervision and deposit insurance The Review then moved on to the prudential settings for deposit takers, and the development of the depositor compensation scheme. This work completed Phase 2, and lead to the enactment of the Deposit Takers Act 2023 on 6 July 2023. 11 The remit can be accessed at: . It is also noted that under the 2021 Act, the Monetary Policy Committee is also bound by a charter and a code of conduct. See the above link for more information. 12 The Reserve Bank board must have regard to the financial policy remit when acting in relation to prudential strategic intentions and standards, as set out in section 49, 2021 Act. 6 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED An overview of the DTA The DTA introduces three significant changes to New Zealand's prudential settings:  Introduces the Depositor Compensation Scheme (the 'DCS'). Once in force, the DCS will protect up to 100,000 per eligible depositor, per institution in the event of a failure. As at the time of its introduction, this is expected to fully protect around 93 percent of depositors.13  Integrates the separate prudential regimes contained in the 1989 Act and the NBDT Act to create a single, consistent framework for the regulation and supervision of financial institutions that essentially engage in the same activity - the business of taking 'deposits' from the public, and lending to individuals, households, and businesses.  Strengthens New Zealand's deposit taker crisis management framework, by mandating the Reserve Bank as the 'resolution authority' with clear statutory purposes, enhancing the powers available to manage a deposit taker in distress and introducing no-creditor worse off provisions. A visual representation of these key changes is as follows (noting that the slide below identifies supervision and enforcement as another key area of the reform): Key areas of DTA reform: UNCLASSIFIED I will now step through these significant changes in some more detail. Starting with the DCS. 13 Press Release, Hon Grant Robertson 'Deposit compensation scheme becomes law', 29 June 2023 7 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED Depositor Compensation Scheme The DCS scheme is the first for New Zealand (noting that the Crown Retail Deposit Guarantee Scheme was temporary opt-in scheme - a creature of contract and the Public Finance Act 1989). However, it is certainly not a world first. According to the International Deposit Insurance Association, globally there are 92 jurisdictions with deposit insurance schemes in place. Currently all OCED countries have deposit insurance except for Israel and New Zealand. The DCS is intended to be up and running by the end of 2024 and will cover 'protected deposits' namely, transactional accounts, savings accounts, and term deposits.14 UNCLASSIFIED Overview of DCS Reserve Bank of New Zealand xx Te POtea Matua Protect eligible depositor up to 100,000 per institution Make payout when a firm goes into liquidation or contributes to resolution measures Totally funded by levy from deposit takers, with Crown backstop Reserve Bank has the functions to collect levy, manage the fund, make payout and provide info to public UNCLASSIFIED Key differences between the old and the new We will now take you through the key differences between the old and the new. The 'old' being the existing prudential regulation regime for registered banks (under the 1989 Act) and for NBDTs (under the NBDT Act). Of course, the old remains the current law, and this will remain the case until the relevant provisions of the DTA come into force. In sum, the 'new' represents a profound paradigm shift in the approach to regulating and supervising entities that are integral to the very important financial system function of credit intermediation. This paradigm shift will bring New Zealand's framework closer to international orthodoxy. The shift is embedded in the new legal foundations provided by the DTA. However, it is also a shift the mindset or philosophy of prudential regulation and supervision by the Reserve Bank when compared to the pre-GFC period. It is one less based on 'trust', and one more built on being proactive, sceptical, and challenging of our regulated population (i.e., trust but verify and show us, 14 Note semantic distinction between 'compensation1 and 'insurance'. A view was taken that the latter does not quite capture the mechanics of the scheme. In addition, the word 'compensation' was recommended to reduce potential confusion for the public vis-a-vis how 'insurance1 is ordinarily understood. But in a practical sense, the DCS does echo the key design choices of deposit insurance schemes globally. 8 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED don't tell us). This approach is underpinned by our Relationship Charter15 and, when a matter is considered by our enforcement function, our Enforcement Framework.16 Our Relationship Charter provides that our communication will be open, clear, targeted, consistent and timely. The key principles of our Enforcement Framework are 'risk-based', 'transparent' and 'proportionate'. Another aspect supporting our on-going paradigm shift is greater funding for the prudential function. This step-up in funding has seen significant investment in the capability and capacity of our staff, and the establishment of a supervisory footprint in Auckland, where many of our regulated entities headquarter their New Zealand operations. Turning to the legal foundations as laid out in the Act. Purposes and principles (Part 1). The DTA is centred on the primacy of financial stability. The main purpose of the DTA is to: promote the prosperity and well-being of New Zealanders and contribute to a sustainable and productive economy by protecting and promoting the stability of the financial system (section 3(1)) This purpose ties into the purpose and financial stability objective in the 2021 Act. Financial stability is a public good and is the best contribution a prudential regulator can make to well-being and prosperity. The DTA also provides what financial stability means for the deposit taking sector through the inclusion of four additional purposes (section 3(2)). The first three of those additional purposes are:  Soundness - to promote the safety and soundness of each deposit taker;  Public confidence - promote public confidence in the financial system; and  Mitigation and management of risks to and from the financial system - to avoid or mitigate the adverse effects of risks to the stability of the financial system and risks from the financial system that may damage the broader economy. To the extent not inconsistent with the main purpose and the first three additional purposes, the fourth additional purpose is:  Accessibility - to support New Zealanders having reasonable access to financial products and services provided by the deposit-taking sector. The accessibility purpose was introduced during the select committee process and, from a legislative standpoint this accessibility purpose is unusual internationally. Multiple purposes for a regulator do create challenges for any regulatory regime, potentially inviting policy trade-offs as 15 Published on the Reserve Bank's website ( ). It sets out principles for maintain the best regulator-regulated relationships possible. The charter is underpinned by the principle of te whakatOpu to bring together, consolidate, and combine our efforts. 16 Published on the Reserve Bank's website ( ). The Enforcement Framework provides guidance on how we act, or propose to act, in relation to our regulated entities, when using our enforcement discretion. The Enforcement Framework consists of several pieces of public guidance which should be read alongside each other to provide an understanding of our enforcement process. 9 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED well as complicating accountability. That said, there is a fail-safe built into the framework as the accessibility purpose is subordinate to financial stability. However, it is not Parliament's intent that the Reserve Bank should pursue financial stability without considering other factors. In other words, the Reserve Bank should not pursue the 'stability of the graveyard', so to speak. There are several decision-making principles (see section 4), that must be taken into account by the Reserve Bank in achieving the purposes of the Act. These include various aspects of financial system efficiency (e.g., maintaining competition), the desirability of taking a proportionate approach to regulation and supervision, as well as supporting the diversity of the deposit taking sector. For completeness, I note that that while the decision-making principles are mandatory considerations that the Reserve Bank must consider, they are not in a legislative sense, policy objectives or outcomes that the Reserve Bank must deliver per se in the way that statutory purposes are. Licensing of deposit takers (Part 2) As mentioned earlier, the DTA integrates two separate regimes and sets the regulatory perimeter for of what entities are prudentially regulated (see the meaning of the term 'deposit taker' in clause 2, Schedule 2). The new regime is activity-based (the business of borrowing and lending), although the Reserve Bank will retain the ability to restrict which deposit takers may use the term 'bank' (sections 428 and 429). Deposit takers that meet certain criteria will need to be licensed by the Reserve Bank. To be issued a licence, an applicant will need to meet certain requirements, which include 'fit and proper' assessments for directors and senior managers (section 17 and subpart 4, Part 2). There will be penalties for an entity conducting business without a licence (see section 11). Holding out offences are also included in the DTA (section 14). There is also flexibility in the new regime for the Reserve Bank to manage the regulatory perimeter through deeming in and exemption provisions. Regulation of deposit takers (Part 3) Standards will replace the current conditions of registration model (for banks) and regulations (for NBDTs). Standards will be secondary legislation under the Legislation Act 2019 (section 72(2)) and, accordingly, will be disallowable instruments that must be presented to by the Minister to Parliament. The DTA provides that a procedure must be followed for issuing standards (section 75), subject to limited exceptions the Reserve Bank must:  notify the Minister of Finance of the propose standard;  consult other members of New Zealand's Council of Financial Regulators (the Financial Markets Authority, the Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment, the Treasury, and the Commerce Commission); and 10 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED  consult persons substantially affected by the issue of a proposed standard. The DTA also provides that the Reserve Bank must prepare and publish a proportionality framework for taking the proportionality principle into account when developing standards (see sections 4(a)(i) and 77). The DTA sets out the subject matters of the standards. The scope is broad and aligns with the expectations of the Basel core principles. The development of these standards will be a major feature of the Reserve Bank's prudential policy work programme in the coming years and will be subject to several rounds of public consultation. In most areas, the Reserve Bank is not envisaging a fundamental redesign of all our existing rules for banks that are already subject to regulation by the Reserve Bank, but there will be areas where our rules need to be updated to reflect the new law, and opportunities to clarify and simplify the rules in some instances. There may also be an opportunity to broaden the rulebook for banks by introducing new requirements they are not currently subject to, for example, around recovery planning and facilitating resolution under Part 7 (section 89). For NBDTs, the existing rules to which they are subject will also be considered to ensure some degree of consistency across the sector, albeit balanced with taking a proportionate approach. Although NBDTs undertake the same or similar activity to banks, they are considerably smaller and less complex than their peers, less systemically important, and have other features that set them apart. It is also relevant to note that NBDTs are currently supervised by trustees; however, under the DTA, the Reserve Bank will assume this responsibility. Proportionality As mentioned earlier, a single regulatory regime means that the Reserve Bank must design standards and other regulatory tools that befit an integrated framework. However, given the diversity of the sector there is a clear rationale for tailoring requirements and adopting a proportionate approach to the calibration of requirements for the wide spectrum of deposit takers. On the supervision front, proportionality will be reflected in a risk-based approach. Indeed, as mentioned above, proportionality is a decision-making principle under the DTA. Further, the Reserve Bank must publish a proportionality framework document to govern the making of Standards. This requirement appears in section 77 of the DTA. The Reserve Bank does not envisage that all, or most, prudential rules will be 'one size fits all' and will be thinking carefully about creating rules that are suitable for the size and other characteristics of these entities, while ensuring the soundness of individual deposit takers. The proportionality framework will assist us to balance the costs and benefits of regulation consistently and transparently in relation to different types of deposit takers, when tailoring the requirements in the standards. 11 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED The purpose of our framework is to group similar deposit takers together after carefully considering:  The size and nature of business of different deposit takers;  Their relative importance to the stability of the financial system; and  The extent to which a range of regulatory requirements are necessary or desirable to promote the safety and soundness of each deposit taker. The framework will not represent an overall lowering of prudential requirements compared to existing regulatory requirements. There will be minimum standards to ensure the safety and soundness of each deposit taker. Due diligence duty Another point of note in Part 3 of the Act is the requirement that directors and New Zealand chief executives (in the case of overseas deposit takers that operate branches in New Zealand) exercise due diligence to ensure the deposit takers complies with its prudential obligations (see sections 93 -97). To comply with this obligation, directors must exercise the care, diligence, and skill that a reasonable director would exercise in the same circumstances, considering the size and nature of business of the deposit taker, and the position of the director and the nature of their responsibilities. The Act provides a meaning of the term due diligence (section 95). The Reserve Bank must also publish guidance about the due diligence duties (section 97). The new directors' duty is modelled off similar duties that can be found in Australia and the UK. These individual liability and accountability regimes were put in place after the GFC so that those individuals that were implicated in institutions failing, at significant cost to taxpayers, could be sanctioned. However, these regimes include key executive positions within banks, whereas the New Zealand framework is focussed on non-executive board members. The formulation of the duty in the Act also closely follows the new duty in section 59B of the CCCFA, including the 'reasonable director' standard and the meaning given to 'due diligence'. Contravention of this duty by an individual could lead to a court imposing a pecuniary penalty up to a maximum of 1,000,000 (section 1578(3)). Although not directly comparable, this is less severe than penalties in the 1989 Act for directors, who could have been imprisoned if they had attested their firm was complying (as part of the public disclosure statement) if this was later found to be incorrect. That said, under the old Act the Reserve Bank has not undertaken any enforcement action against bank directors, which raises questions as to how credible the old approach to self-discipline was. The new regime is intended to be easier to enforce, more proportionate in terms of the sanction, and arguably a more credible way of incentivising directors to internalise the negative consequences of their firm's risk-taking activities. 12 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED Supervision and Enforcement (Parts 4 and 5) The DTA provides new supervision and enforcement tools and powers to support a more proactive approach to assessing compliance, and a more proportionate sanctioning regime to deal with non-compliance. These powers are intended to provide more tailored, proportionate, and efficient outcomes when compared to the supervisory and enforcement toolkits under the old legislation. Some of the most significant aspects of this modernised took kit are outlined below. Rebalancing towards pecuniary penalties The DTA rebalances away from the current emphasis on criminal penalties in the old legislation. The DTA contains civil pecuniary penalties for breaches of prudential standards (section 157). The maximum amount these pecuniary penalties for a body corporate will be the greater of 5,000,000 and 0.1% of total assets of the group; and 1,000,000 for individuals (section 158). Criminal penalties still exist in the new legislation but are now more targeted for deliberate non- compliance with directions and other intentional wrongdoing. For example, knowing contravention of a confidentiality order (section 132); intentional contravention of a banning order (section 180) etc. On-site inspections The DTA also provides that the Reserve Bank may conduct on-site inspections for specified purposes (section 112). Almost all jurisdictions provide for the ability of the prudential regulator to undertake on-site inspections, many without prior notice. Information garnered through on-sites will complement that gained through on-going desk-based supervision and monitoring. During an on-site, the Reserve Bank can require employees, directors, and agents of deposit takers to answer questions and provide information. It will be an offence to refuse to comply or otherwise obstruct the inspection. There is also the power under the DTA to appoint an investigator who will be able to compel the provision of information - including the questioning of any director, employee, or any other person, under oath or affirmation (sections 126 -127). Other more targeted tools The DTA also contains several other more targeted supervision and enforcement tools to provide for a more appropriate response to various types of non-compliance. The Reserve Bank may issue remedial notices (section 119) and accept enforceable undertakings with deposit takers (section 148). The Act also contains several infringement offences for low level non-compliance (e.g., failure provide a fit and proper certificate - section 31). In terms of how the Reserve Bank will approach these new powers, I refer to our Enforcement Framework, which we completed earlier this year and in available on our website. The Framework is the Reserve Bank's enforcement policy, which provides guidance on how we propose to act when considering and pursuing enforcement matters. Our three key principles are 13 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED transparent, proportionate and risk based. It currently applies to the old legislation, and it will be updated as needed to operationalise this new enforcement tool kit when it comes into force. Crisis management and resolution (Part 7) The DTA provides an updated crisis management and resolution framework and establishes the Reserve Bank as the 'resolution authority' for all licensed deposit takers. Once in force, this new regime will replace the statutory management regime for registered banks provided for in the 1989 Act. Statutory management under the Corporations (Investigation and Management) Act 1989 will remain a possibility for licensed deposit takers, as well the application of the other New Zealand insolvency regimes (liquidation, receivership etc.), as appropriate in the circumstances. An overview of Part 7 is as follows. Additional purposes Part 7 contains additional purposes (over and above the main purpose and additional purposes in section 4). These are set out in section 259 and cover avoiding damage to the financial system, ensuring a deposit taker can be resolved in an orderly manner, supporting the purposes of the DCS, and a subordinate purpose tied to managing the risks to public funds. Resolution planning requirements Under the DTA, the Reserve Bank must prepare and maintain a resolution plan for each deposit taker (section 260) and publish a Statement of Resolution Approach (section 262). This will set out our expected strategies for dealing with failing deposit takers, and our intended approach to co- operating and engaging with relevant agencies, both domestically and internationally. Pre-resolution powers Several pre-resolution powers are provided in Part 7. These include a direction power, a power to appoint/remove directors and to approve the sale or disposition of a deposit taker (sections 265 - 270). Resolution regime If a deposit taker meets the non-viability and necessity grounds to be placed into resolution (section 280), the resolution regime will apply. The resolution regime contains several tools and features like those contained in the 1989 Act statutory management regime (for example, the moratorium and the carve outs and stays for certain rights under netting agreements, derivatives, and rules of designated FMIs) (sections 284- 297). However, there are some key differences -the Reserve Bank must act as the resolution authority to further the Part 7 purposes and regularly report to the Minister of Finance on the conduct of the resolution (section 298, 299 and 301). The Reserve Bank and supervise the resolution manager to ensure they efficiently and effectively perform their functions, powers, and duties (section 300). The resolution powers have also been modernised to better align with international resolution regimes. The Financial Stability Board's Key Attributes of Effective Resolution 14 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED Regimes for Financial System were closely considered in the development of the resolution regime in the DTA. No-creditor or shareholder worse-off The Act provides a mechanism to compensate shareholders and creditors of entities in resolution where they are worse off in a resolution when compared to their treatment in a liquidation (sections 367 - 402). The 'No Creditor Worse Off' mechanism recognises that resolution powers could potentially be used in ways that disadvantage certain creditors of the failed deposit taker. The existence of the safeguard should encourage decision makers to exercise resolution powers in a way that ensures all creditors receive at least what they would have received in in a normal insolvency process such as liquidation. Contribution to resolution from the DCS fund The DTA provides that in certain prescribed circumstances, the DCS fund may be used to support a resolution measure (section 199). Very briefly, this means that in some cases the Reserve Bank may consider it more appropriate to use resolution powers to stabilise the troubled institution. In these cases, the Act provides for a payment to be made from the DCS fund to contribute to the resolution strategy, to the extent that no more funds are provided than would have been used in the DCS payout for that institution. In preparation for Part 7 coming into force under the DTA, the Reserve Bank is currently undertaking policy work to explore optimal resolution strategies for different cohorts of deposit takers. This work will include a further consideration of the potential role for statutory bail-in powers, upon which we are expected to report back to the Minister of Finance within the next two years. Next steps - the journey to 'full force' The journey to bring the DTA into force will be a long one. The Reserve Bank's current planning will see full implementation in July 2028, a year before the backstop provided for in the Act of July 2029. The DCS will be put in place first. It is expected to come into force in late 2024 (October). Following the publication of the proportionality framework in early 2024, standards will be developed and consulted on from then until 2026, with licensing under the DTA occurring in 2027 prior to full commencement in July 2028. As this is a long process, dates will likely change over time. For the latest updates please check the Council of Financial Regulators, Regulatory Initiatives Calendar17 which is updated quarterly. Our consultation over this time with be a combination of published documents for seeking feedback through submissions and workshops with industry to discuss proposals. The following slide demonstrates the timeline based on current assumptions. 17 15 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3 UNCLASSIFIED 2023 I 2029 DEPOSIT TAKERS ACT ROLL OUT (current assumption) IN CONFIDENCE Conclusion I started this paper by promising to cover three points - the key bones of the DTA, how it differs from its predecessor legislation and what industry can expect in terms of how we now go about bringing the DTA into full force. I will end this paper by briefly summarising those points. The framework (or skeleton) of the DTA is clear - we can simply read the Act itself. However, for deeper context and to gain an understand of what has informed the DTA (and its place in the matrix of New Zealand and global financial regulation), I suggest it is helpful to pause and look back. Perhaps not as far as 1668, but at least back to 1989. The DTA differs from its predecessor legislation by providing modern statutory foundations that embed a profound shift in the mindset or philosophy to prudential regulation and supervision of New Zealand deposit takers - especially when compared to the pre-GFC period. This shift brings New Zealand's framework and approach closer to international best practice. Open, clear, targeted, consistent, and timely communication underpins the Reserve Bank's approach to this shift. The journey in bringing the DTA into full force will take several years and will be a major part of the Reserve Banks prudential work programme over the coming years. There will be several rounds of public consultation on the materials which are necessary to 'colour in' what the DTA means for all stakeholders. The proportionality framework, DCS regulations, prudential standards, and the statement of resolution approach are all crucial to provide depth and certainty going forward for all stakeholders. The Reserve Bank looks forward to engaging with your all on this journey, to promote the prosperity and well-being of New Zealanders and contribute to a sustainable and productive economy. 16 (Another) Seismic Shift in New Zealand: Banking regulatory reform - the Deposit Takers Act 2023 UNCLASSIFIED Ref #20571475 v2.3

Title: Fair and reasonable response to mushrooming OIA requests
text: Fair and reasonable response to mushrooming OIA requests By Geoff Bascand, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of New Zealand The Reserve Bank has established a policy on when it will charge for responses to Official Information Act (OIA) requests that has drawn the ire of some critics. Far from it being An obstacle in the path of freedom that the DomPost editorial writer claimed (18 January), the policy is a common, fair and reasonable response to a marked growth of OIA requests. Id like to explain our rationale, and what the policy means for requesters  most of whom will likely not be charged. Our approach is consistent with the Official Information Act and meets the Banks commitment to transparency. Like all public sector organisations, the Reserve Bank must promote public accountability by providing proper access to information, unless there are good reasons to protect it. We publish most responses to OIA requests for universal access. Official organisations  and therefore taxpayers and ratepayers  usually bear the cost of providing responses to OIA requests, but the Official Information Act recognises that some requests can be so onerous that responding lies beyond the organisations normal resources. In these circumstances, the Ombudsman considers it is reasonable that requesters bear some of the associated costs. We have considered several cases when: requests are for very large amounts of information; a response to a request is particularly complex; or a requester makes frequent requests. Over the past five years, we have seen an increase in OIA requests of almost 300 percent, several of which have taken many days of work. Like other public sector agencies, our budget is tightly constrained. When developing the policy, we liaised with the Office of the Ombudsman and examined other agencies policies. Our policy is consistent with the Ministry of Justice Guidelines for the public sector on charging. While the policy applies to all OIA requests, in practice we will seek charges when requests are large, complex, or frequent. Importantly, it requires us to work with the requester to refine their request to a scale that is less likely to incur costs. We expect most requests will not incur charges. We have taken an even-handed approach: charges are based on the volume of work required to provide information, and it applies equally to individuals, trade and industry bodies, companies, news media, bloggers, etc. Since the policy was introduced weve responded to seven OIA requests and sought charges for two of them because most could be addressed without collating large amounts of information. The particular charge that sparked recent commentary arose because providing the information requested would take an estimated 8 hours of chargeable time (along with additional nonchargeable time). We gave the requester several opportunities to refine the request so that 6414836 v1.8 2 charges would be cut or eliminated. He chose to withdraw the request rather than refine it any further. We can reduce or waive charges if they might cause financial hardship for the requester, or if releasing the information is likely to contribute significantly to public understanding of the Reserve Bank and its work. A balanced approach with reasonable charges for large requests for information and a willingness to work with requestors seems unlikely to imperil democracy in New Zealand. Instead it makes these easier to manage, and helps the Bank fulfil the OIA in making valuable information publically available. 6414836 v1.8

Title: Engaging with our stakeholders to promote understanding, accountability and dialogue
text: Engaging with our stakeholders to promote understanding, accountability and dialogue A speech delivered to the Canterbury branch of the Institute of Directors in Christchurch Released 27 June 2017 By Mike Hannah, Head of Communications 2 The Terrace, PO Box 2498, Wellington 6140, New Zealand Telephone 64 4 472 2029 Online at 2 Reflecting our range of responsibilities as a central bank, the Reserve Bank engages widely with a diverse range of stakeholders, from governance relationships, financial institutions and markets, to the media, the general public and educators. The Bank treats each of these relationships seriously. We apply considerable senior resource to maintaining relationships, our engagement, and communications. We also recognise that each group has its own specific interests and expectations of the Bank. Our engagements occur against a backdrop of not only an ever-changing economic and financial environment, but also substantial demographic changes among those we interact with. These can range from the outcomes of a general election for our Parliamentary stakeholders, to the ongoing fundamental disruption in the news media sector that has delivered kaleidoscopic changes to media outlets and journalists with whom we engage. New banks, insurers and other financial institutions arrive, while others retire. The Bank takes the pulse of these relationships informally very frequently, from both management and governance perspectives, and I will talk of those health checks today. In addition, we decided in 2015 that we would take an in-depth assessment every three to four years, through an External Stakeholder Engagement Survey, after we had conducted our first such survey in late 2014/early 2015. We undertook this first survey because communication is important to the success of our policy objectives to facilitate wide understanding of what we do (and dont do). How people perceive us is informative as to how clearly our messages are being received and understood, and where we may need to tailor our efforts better. There are three essential reasons why the Reserve Bank communicates, and endeavours to do so transparently: - to demonstrate accountability for its degree of autonomy or independence in pursuing policy objectives; - to promote understanding, so as to enhance the credibility and effectiveness of policy; and - to use communication to signal its intended action, so informing and shaping expectations of policy actions. The success of our policies relies heavily on the behaviours of households, businesses and other stakeholders being consistent with those policy objectives. For instance, widespread understanding of the goal and operation of monetary policy makes it easier to achieve and maintain price stability, by better anchoring low inflation expectations. This means that wage and price setters are more confident in the Banks focus and, in turn, that the Bank is able to respond to economic shocks by adjusting interest rates less than would otherwise be the case. Similarly, understanding of our macro-prudential policies can help to anchor expectations of credit growth to the desired goal of financial stability, and so reduce the risk of damaging asset booms and busts. Our banking supervision is also supported by broad understanding that we do not guarantee that no financial institution will fail, and creditors and depositors will know to adjust their behaviour to risks. 3 Confidence in New Zealands banknotes is supported by one of the broadest engagement programmes the Bank has undertaken to ensure that people are aware of the security and design features of the banknotes in introducing the Series Seven banknotes in 2015-16. While effective communication of our messages is vital to our goals, listening to our many communities of interest is also crucial. We will undertake a second External Stakeholder Engagement Survey in the first half of 2018  capturing representatives of groups such as yours again  so it is timely at this point to recall some of the results of the first survey, the changes to the landscape we are operating in, and our responses. A key takeout from the 2014 Stakeholder Survey was just how different the various groups we interact with are from each other in their perceptions and expectations of their relationships with the Bank, and, therefore, the care that we need to take to engage with each group in its own context and language. The groups that we surveyed were: - General public - Media - Business - Regulated industry - Markets/analysts - Education/researchers - Government The survey was undertaken by polling and research firm, Ipsos New Zealand. They applied a framework across the perceptions of each of its key stakeholder groups, assessing reputation and credibility. This framework was based on:  Familiarity  The extent to which the Reserve Bank is familiar to stakeholders in terms of activities, benefits, values, mission.  Favourability  The extent to which the Reserve Bank is viewed positively.  Trust  Ultimately trust underpins reputation. Without trust, messages are rejected. Build trust and you build support, your messages are better received, and ultimately you gain advocates.  Advocacy  The extent to which stakeholders will actively speak highly or critically of the Reserve Bank. 4 Seen as a reputation pyramid, one element lays the foundation for a higher level of engagement above: Advocacy Trust Favourability Familiarity The survey found that trust  a necessary foundation for the credibility and acceptance of the Banks messages  goes hand-in-hand with familiarity  i.e., an understanding of the Bank, its policies and activities. It also revealed a material divergence between general public and more specialist stakeholder groups perceptions of the Bank. This gap, and other differences between stakeholder perceptions, have had a significant influence on where and how the Bank has sought to engage externally over the last two-anda-half years  even taking into account the changing environment in which we operate. That is evident if we look at each of the stakeholder groups separately. 5 General public  What the 2014 Survey told us: The survey found that the public is generally trusting, albeit at a lower level than more specialist stakeholder groups, and that trust is based on very low familiarity. Generally, the public identified themselves as interested only where the Bank directly affects them, e.g. the Official Cash Rate, Loan-to-Value lending limits. Engagement is mostly through third parties such as the media, or their bank or other regulated industries. When the public see a positive link between what the Reserve Bank does and the economy and their own financial wellbeing they are more positive.  What we have done: Our response to these findings has been shaped significantly by both the measured gap in the publics understanding of the Bank, and the changes in traditional news media as digital media has grown. News media business models have been fundamentally challenged by the attraction of advertising revenue to the likes of giant web platforms such Google and Yahoo. In addition, global sources of news are more readily accessed via the web, so consumers of news and commentary have more choice and can readily customise their news sources. The importance for our public stakeholders is that news media were identified in the survey as a key traditional intermediary between the Bank and the general public. At this stage, I want to illustrate the increasing work we have done to connect with the general public directly, via the web and other digital and social media channels. I will then talk more about our engagement with news media. The Bank has long issued an extensive range of publications for broad and specialist consumption to facilitate understanding of what the Bank does. These include Bulletin articles and Analytical Notes on current research topics, through to highly technical Discussion Papers aimed at the central banking and academic research community. For public affairs nowadays to be conducted effectively, agencies recognise the need to participate in digital channels, given their reach into communities. Currently, the Bank has its main website, which fronts our digital platforms, principally YouTube, Twitter, and more recently SoundCloud, with some use of Facebook. YouTube The Bank has been using YouTube to host videos and animations for seven years. We currently have 121 videos on our YouTube channel. 6 Many of these videos explain the Banks roles or operations (e.g., inflation, stress tests, macro-prudential tools, banknotes etc.). We also routinely post videos of the press conferences after the release of Monetary Policy Statements and Financial Stability Reports, as well as short highlight videos of these webcasts. Each year we also post footage of the finalists presentations for the Monetary Policy Challenge. Twitter The Bank began using Twitter in late 2012. In that time, weve issued 328 tweets and gained 5061 followers. Those are not large numbers, but we know we reach far wider audiences as some of our followers re-tweet to many thousands of their followers. Most of our tweets are the headlines of news releases we issue followed by a link to the news release on our website. We also promote some one-off content  like new videos or publications. Facebook The Bank primarily uses Facebook to communicate to participants of our secondary school economics competition, the Monetary Policy Challenge (MPC). The Banks MPC page currently has 339 followers and is largely used to provide updates, announcements and reminders about the competition. However, we also used a Brighter Money Facebook page to promote the new Series Seven banknotes, as part of our educational campaign. Familiarity with the security and design features of banknotes is one the strongest mitigants against counterfeiting, so reaching wide audiences is paramount. While the posts and page were well received and had good engagement from thousands of users, they generated a lot of comments on posts that we did not have the resource to respond to. SoundCloud We began using SoundCloud  a music and audio social media platform  earlier this year, and since then have posted 10 pieces of audio. These are predominately recordings of the MPS and FSR press statements, but we have also uploaded interviews with Bulletin authors and speeches. Our audio has been listened to 550 times, with the bulk of listeners in New Zealand, followed by the United States. Audiences Social media channels offer a diverse range of audiences. A majority of our Twitter followers (60 percent) are aged between 25 and 34, but we have comparatively fewer younger followers aged under 24 than the average Twitter publishers. That may reflect the age profile of people when they commonly become interested in saving and borrowing and, therefore, have an interest in interest rates. Some 83 percent are male and 17 percent are female. The reason for the gender imbalance is less clear: it may be due to the way the industry captures analytics, and it may reflect the fact that the age group we attract in the financial sector is male-dominated. Geographically, 37 percent are based in New Zealand, followed by 12 percent in the United States and 9 percent in Australia. About 12 percent of followers reside in Auckland and 8 percent in Canterbury. 7 Similar demographic trends are reflected among our YouTube audience, but with a trend towards younger viewers. This demographic information suggests that Twitter and YouTube are probably very effective channels to reach middle-aged audiences who already have an interest in business and finance, but probably less effective if we want to communicate messages to younger (particularly school-aged) audiences, or people closer to retirement age. OCR or MPS-related tweets are our most re-tweeted messages. We are moving, where possible, to including images or videos with tweets, as these are more engaging, and our followers are more likely to interact with them and share them. Our educational campaign last year to familiarise New Zealanders with the new banknotes and their security features gave the Bank a rare opportunity to engage through other communication channels. We recognised that our objective would be achieved better by reaching as wide an audience as possible. This included social radio. In collaboration with one of the main media organisations, NZME (publishers of the NZ Herald and owners of a number of radio stations), we engaged radio presenters in very short comic video skits to highlight some of the security features. The approach generated large audiences. We also used native advertising  a sponsored story and a banknote quiz on Stuffs website. Some 9000 people filled in the quiz, making it Stuffs most completed quiz, and achieved 118 million impressions across the banners, adverts and content drivers that encouraged people to click through to the Brighter Money website. Of these impressions, 18,000 people did click through to the website. We are told this is above the industry standard. Using these channels for what a Governor once called our most popular product, banknotes, is one thing  doing so with more contentious policy material is another, and we are still feeling our way. These digital channels are designed to offer explanations of our policy and activities in more accessible, less technical language than is required for formal policy or regulatory statements. They are mostly visual, so as to attract more attention. They are complementary to the outreach we undertake through the news media and our face-to-face presentations. Our social media is used more sparingly in comparison to other government organisations, but is as active as many other central banks. One reason why we are different from some New Zealand agencies  such as NZ Police, the New Zealand Defence Force, the Ministry for Primary Industries, and Department of Internal Affairs  is that the Bank does not have a direct customer or transactional relationship with the general public as these agencies have. We operate through intermediaries, that is, other financial institutions and agents who issue mortgages, take deposits, or provide access to banknotes. In that sense, we are more akin to a business-to-business (B2B) relationship in the commercial world. A direct transactional relationship tends to see more web and social media development. While the Reserve Bank is active in several social media channels, we have been cautious in opening up the two-way engagement that is typical of some channels. This means we have not taken the opportunity to follow other users, or respond to comments on our content, or share other peoples content, nor to answer social media questions publicly. This has been partly because of the risk of having our statements in an informal channel being 8 read as public signals. There are also reputational risks that a central bank has to be conscious of. A quick informal comment on Twitter or Facebook can quickly attract unintended negative reactions and go viral, and the resulting storm distracts us from our core business. However, the uptake and speed of growth of digital technologies has reinforced the need to be aware of trends, and to adopt those technologies that best suit the Banks roles and relationships. We actively explore these potential opportunities and look to how we can invest in them. By doing so, the Bank will be able to utilise the most effective and up-to-date strategies, platforms and technologies to communicate with a broad range of stakeholders on all its messages. The key insight for us has been not only to be present and active within these spheres, but to continue to stay abreast of developing trends, such as app developments or, who knows, even AR (Augmented reality) and VR (Virtual reality) technologies. We have already been approached to create AR and VR apps but havent progressed these proposals yet. Media  What the 2014 Survey told us: The survey told us that the Media seek frequent and open access and a deeper understanding of the rationale and background to decision making.  What we have done: For the news media, a particular challenge has been the disruption to the sector from internet competition, restructuring the face of the sector enormously. This is a global phenomenon. So also has been an increasing scrutiny of financial authorities since the Global Financial Crisis. Although the New Zealand economy and financial system performed well during the Global Financial Crisis, we are subject to the same scrutiny as other financial authorities in more troubled economies. The news media landscape continues to undergo rapid and large-scale change. New players continue to emerge in the New Zealand media scene. They are typically small and low-cost, without the legacy operations found in many traditional media companies. While these new players are all relatively early-stage companies, they indicate that there is still a demand for news that may not be being met by some media outlets. At the same time, traditional media have become multi-channel, so that the distinction between print, radio and TV has blurred with most mainstream media offering text, audio and video options. We maintain a close watch on developments in the media sector, as channels may open or close for our communications to the public and other stakeholders. 9 While we have seen the loss of several familiar faces among journalists in the rounds of restructurings, we have seen less change than some reporting spheres due to the more specialist nature of good quality economic and financial journalism. Nevertheless, we are conscious of the pressure that a smaller number of journalists are under to produce more, short stories for multi-channel delivery. This puts a premium on the time those journalists have with the Bank to maintain an understanding of what we are doing and why. Relationships In this context, it is understandable, therefore, that, where the Bank has chosen or felt compelled to restrict access to journalists, tensions have arisen with the media. Two developments since the 2014 survey was taken are worthy of mention here. First is the nature of our engagements with business audiences around the country. We provide around 120 presentations a year to business audiences, going out to pretty well all New Zealand cities and towns with a population of more than 20,000, and some even smaller. The events are all off-the-record, though for a dozen or so, like todays event here, we will publish a formal speech text when we have particular messages to deliver to financial markets, institutions or broader audiences. Incidentally, the number of on-the-record speeches will always vary according to the need for public messaging. We published 15 on-the-record speeches in 2016, eight in 2015, and 18 in 2014. These speeches are delivered predominantly by the Banks Governors, recognising the important role of the Governing Committee. This Committee was an innovation in our decision-making process in 2013, and brings the Banks four Governors together as a policy decision-making group, while the Governor remains accountable for those decisions. As a committee, the Governors Committee benefits decision making by pooling the knowledge and expertise of individual Governors, which is particularly valuable where there is uncertainty and in mitigating the risk of extreme preferences of an individual. As a collective, it rigorously tests ideas and builds consensus around major policy decisions. Since its inception, we have also developed the Banks speaking engagements around all four Governors to reflect the Committees consensus role. In terms of the off-the-record presentations, media may occasionally attend some of these events as members of the host organisation or when invited by the Bank  such as to our Boards outreach functions  but still on the basis that what is said at the event, by the Bank or the audience, is not reportable. Generally, however, media are not invited to the wider programme of events. We can understand why the media may find this frustrating  they have a natural interest in a potential story; or why they may be even suspicious  why would we speak off-the-record if its not because we are saying something sensitive? In both cases, the perception would be misplaced. We have held these events for over 25 years now under the same circumstances. The Bank has a well-established protocol that when it has market-sensitive messages to deliver, it will publish them first so that financial market participants have an equal opportunity to receive the messages at the same time. These 120 events are off the record so as to allow the Bank to listen to and have a conversation with business audiences, in their own context and language. To enable more accessibility and engagement with the audience, our language and approach is informal, and will often depart from the strict, coded language of our formal statements that financial 10 markets monitor minutely. We are not delivering different messages from what we have said publicly, but presenting mainly on the material recently delivered in the Monetary Policy Statements and Financial Stability Reports. But being away from financial market monitoring allows us to use business-friendly language and explanations, without that language being interpreted as a change of policy signalling. At the same time, it gives businesses the freedom to raise questions of clarification or to share information with us about their businesses and environment. So we do not see these off-the-record events as a story but as vehicles for enhancing understanding, even educational. To place all of these events on the record risks creating frequent and distracting market noise and closing down the audience interaction. We also have occasionally held off-the-record briefings for various media, generally in Wellington and Auckland, on issues they wish to raise with us. These vary in frequency, and more recently we have leaned more towards presenting them as on-the-record briefings for media to explain important publications  particular economic analysis, for instance, or a statistical release. We have adopted this approach to facilitate our material in reaching a wider audience, but also to encourage the growth of more of a two-way public dialogue with the media. The journalists come away with a story, we come away with wider media knowledge of what the Bank is doing, and both of us come away, we hope, with more understanding between ourselves. However, we were compelled to cease one long-standing off-the-record engagement with news media just over a year ago. We had held off-the-record lock-ups for journalists ahead of the release of MPSs, OCR Statements and FSRs. During this time, the media in the lockup had access to the sensitive documents under embargo. This was to enable the journalists to read the documents and to prepare their stories ready for release at the end of an embargo and ahead of a press conference. A leak of the March 2016 MPS from the media lock-up led us to halt all such lock-ups. Regardless of technology or long-standing trust, the leak meant that we could not guarantee to financial market participants that information could not be leaked again. Only a very few central banks provide such lock-up arrangements, and they have invested heavily in technology to minimise the risk of leakage. They also have more control to block communication traffic than we have as we share our building with tenants. Given we are the tenth most traded currency in the world, and we are not confident that we can have a technologically secure environment, the reputational stakes are very high. We listened to counter-arguments from many journalists and media groups, but the reputational risk for the central bank outweighed the relationship risk with the media, and the lock-ups have not been reinstated. We instead now first publicly release our statements, following this up an hour later with a live-streamed, questions-and-answers, media conference, and then a varying number of one-on-one interviews with the four Governors who make up the Governing Committee. The decision to halt these lock-ups negatively affected the Banks relationships with news reporters. Media told us that what they felt they had lost most was access to the Bank. We appreciate this, and recognise that access is a powerful tool to enable understanding and scrutiny of the Banks activities. In response, we have increased the number of interviews with the four Governors, and we have made some briefings on-the-record. We keep the potential use of other briefings for media under active consideration. 11 Business  What the 2014 Survey told us: The survey revealed that Business expressed high trust in the Bank, but low familiarity, and a lower perception of relevance. To build greater engagement, communication with this group must be relevant and actionable. Business networks valued the closer relationship that they have, compared with individual businesses.  What we have done: Face-to-face communication still key While there is a large emphasis on innovative technologies, social media and other media platforms, face-to-face communication remains an integral part of how we reach out. We recognise there is still a strong appetite for human interaction rather than receiving information via digital platforms, or what one commentator has called a cellular facade. As I mentioned earlier, the Bank provides about 120 presentations a year to business audiences. Most are delivered by the Governors. Since the Engagement Survey was taken, over the last three years the volume has been consistently higher than in the past. These events present valuable opportunities for the Bank to listen to a large number of stakeholders, mainly in New Zealand. Where we can, we opt for a format where we make a short economic presentation and have a long question-and-answer session between the speaker and the audience. These sessions can cover questions on the Banks wide areas of responsibility (and some areas beyond our responsibility!). The size of the audience varies anywhere from 30 to 600, so it can be a very important vehicle for open dialogue. In 2016, 109 of these were delivered in New Zealand and 12 overseas. That is very similar to 2015 where respectively 112 and 15 were delivered. The numbers do not include the wide range of forums, briefings and other external sessions that our staff participate in each year, including scores of visits to individual businesses around our quarterly economic forecasting rounds, where we seek businesses assessments of their conditions. The numbers do include functions hosted by our Board of Directors in main centres in New Zealand. These presentations are preceded by a social function, allowing local businesses and educators to talk directly with our Directors and senior staff. Local news media are invited on an off-the-record basis, though fewer attend these days, possibly reflecting the pressure on journalists time. 12 The programme of presentations is built throughout the year, with the release of the four MPSs and two FSRs providing a key focus for events. We aim to achieve wide regional spread. In almost all cases, we are hosted by a business networking organisation that provides the event for their members. To build still greater engagement, we have increased our stakeholder contact with some hosts (e.g. union and employer organisations) by holding small group briefings of 10-20 attendees, coupled with a main presentation. The host invites key members to attend. This has created more dialogue and a chance for participants to discuss specialist topics relevant to their business. The programme has the added benefit of giving our senior economic analysts face-to-face engagement with business audiences. We have also used the programme to focus more attention on financial stability developments covered in the FSRs. This has included speaking engagements, as well as analysts briefings. 13 Regulated Industries  What the 2014 Survey told us: The 2014 Survey told us that relationships between the Reserve Bank and registered banks are mature, characterised by high trust and high familiarity. Banks seek earlier and more dialogue around policy, an extension of trust. Insurers and NBDT relationships are emerging, characterised by high levels of familiarity, but lower levels of trust. They seek early consultation and dialogue, and opportunities to engage and influence.  What we have done: The regulated sector  banks, non-bank deposit takers, insurers  told us that they would like earlier consultation and to work together ahead of new regulation. This feedback was perhaps not too surprising from the household mortgage sector, coming soon after the introduction of loan-to-value speed limits on mortgage lending. Regulation is not always a popular side of government  after all, by definition it restricts what some entities may want to do. Since 2014, we have adapted our process for consulting on regulatory initiatives, in order to improve transparency and industry engagement. We have responded to industry concerns about the variable length of consultation periods by publicly committing to a default 8-10 week period (which can be shorter if the matter is urgent). We produce quarterly newsletters for the banking and insurance industry, explaining recent and forthcoming developments in each sector. As part of preparing our Financial Stability Reports, we have also introduced a liaison programme with the banking sector, where we meet with senior staff and product managers to discuss topics of interest, such as credit conditions, funding, and market demand. We also meet with some non-bank stakeholders. We now use workshops with regulated entities for many policy proposals and when developing new statistical collections, most recently when we re-developed our extensive statistics on bank balance sheets. This interaction is vital in helping us to better understand measurement issues, bank systems and practices that have an important bearing on the information that can be provided.
